  • First Nations Pedagogy Online: https://opentextbc.ca/indigenizationfrontlineworkers/

docs.title: Verification Checklist
docs.text:
After completing indigenous knowledge analysis, verify:

  • Grounded in respect and acknowledgment of indigenous territories and peoples
  • Identified specific indigenous nation(s) or community(ies) (avoided pan-indigenous generalizations)
  • Centered indigenous voices and perspectives
  • Applied relational analysis (interconnections, reciprocity, relationships)
  • Evaluated intergenerational impacts (seven generations principle)
  • Conducted holistic wellness assessment across four dimensions
  • Analyzed indigenous rights and sovereignty (FPIC, treaties, self-determination, UNDRIP)
  • Integrated traditional knowledge where appropriate and with permission
  • Considered colonial context and decolonization implications
  • Acknowledged positionality and limitations (especially for non-indigenous analysts)
  • Deferred to indigenous leadership on solutions and pathways forward
  • Used culturally respectful language and terminology
  • Cited indigenous sources and scholars

docs.title: Common Pitfalls to Avoid
docs.text:
Pitfall 1: Pan-Indigenous Generalizations

  • Problem: Treating all indigenous peoples as homogeneous; ignoring diversity of nations, cultures, languages, and perspectives
  • Solution: Specify which nation or community; acknowledge diversity; avoid "indigenous people believe..."

Pitfall 2: Romanticization or Essentialism

  • Problem: Portraying indigenous peoples as mystical, frozen in time, or inherently spiritual; "noble savage" stereotype
  • Solution: Recognize indigenous peoples as contemporary, diverse, and dynamic; avoid stereotypes

Pitfall 3: Non-Indigenous Analysts Speaking for Indigenous Peoples

  • Problem: Centering non-indigenous interpretations over indigenous voices; claiming to know what's best for indigenous communities
  • Solution: Amplify indigenous voices; acknowledge limitations; defer to indigenous leadership

Pitfall 4: Appropriation of Indigenous Knowledge

  • Problem: Extracting and using indigenous knowledge without permission, credit, or benefit-sharing; treating knowledge as free resource
  • Solution: Respect intellectual and cultural property rights; seek permission; acknowledge sources; ensure benefit flows to communities

Pitfall 5: Ignoring Colonial Context

  • Problem: Analyzing issues as if colonization is historical rather than ongoing; missing power structures and systemic oppression
  • Solution: Center colonialism and its ongoing impacts; analyze power relations; consider decolonization

Pitfall 6: Superficial Consultation

  • Problem: Token consultation without genuine power-sharing; "we consulted" without indigenous control over decisions
  • Solution: Distinguish consultation from consent; advocate for Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) and indigenous decision-making authority

Pitfall 7: Applying Western Frameworks Without Critique

  • Problem: Using only Western analytical tools; forcing indigenous knowledge into Western categories; privileging Western science
  • Solution: Center indigenous frameworks; use Two-Eyed Seeing to integrate knowledge systems respectfully; critique Western knowledge hegemony

Pitfall 8: Focusing Only on Problems, Not Strengths

  • Problem: Deficit-focused analysis that emphasizes trauma, poverty, social problems without recognizing resilience, resistance, and cultural vitality
  • Solution: Acknowledge challenges AND strengths; recognize indigenous agency, resilience, and resistance; celebrate cultural revitalization

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
A quality indigenous knowledge analysis:

  • Centers indigenous voices, knowledge, and leadership
  • Specifies which indigenous nation(s) or community(ies) are affected
  • Applies relational thinking and interconnection analysis
  • Uses seven generations principle for intergenerational assessment
  • Conducts holistic wellness evaluation across four dimensions
  • Analyzes indigenous rights, sovereignty, and self-determination
  • Considers colonial context and decolonization implications
  • Integrates traditional knowledge respectfully and with permission
  • Acknowledges analyst positionality and limitations
  • Defers to indigenous leadership for solutions and decisions
  • Avoids appropriation, romanticization, and pan-indigenous generalizations
  • Uses culturally respectful language and protocols
  • Cites indigenous sources and scholars
  • Recognizes both challenges and strengths/resilience
  • Provides actionable insights aligned with indigenous values and rights

docs.title: Integration with Other Analysts
docs.text:
Indigenous knowledge analysis complements other disciplinary perspectives:

  • Environmentalist: Adds traditional ecological knowledge, relational ethics, seven generations principle to environmental analysis
  • Historian: Provides long-term temporal perspective, oral history, and decolonial lens on historical events
  • Political Scientist: Adds sovereignty, self-determination, and decolonization frameworks to political analysis
  • Economist: Challenges extractive economics; offers alternative frameworks (reciprocity, collective wellbeing, intergenerational responsibility)
  • Sociologist: Adds collective and relational dimensions; challenges individualism; provides community-based perspectives

Indigenous analysis is particularly strong on:

  • Relationality and interconnection
  • Intergenerational thinking and long-term sustainability
  • Holistic integration across dimensions
  • Decolonization and sovereignty
  • Traditional ecological knowledge
  • Collective wisdom and community-based approaches

docs.title: Continuous Improvement
docs.text:
This skill evolves as:

  • Indigenous scholars and communities share knowledge and frameworks
  • Decolonization advances and indigenous sovereignty is restored
  • Traditional knowledge is revitalized and transmitted intergenerationally
  • Non-indigenous people learn to listen and defer to indigenous leadership
  • Institutional practices shift toward respect for indigenous rights and knowledge

Important Note: This skill is offered with humility and recognition that indigenous knowledge is held by indigenous peoples and communities. Non-indigenous use of this skill must center indigenous voices, respect protocols, and support indigenous self-determination.

Share feedback and learnings to enhance this skill over time.

Skill Status: Pass 1 Complete - Comprehensive Foundation Established Next Steps: Community review and feedback for cultural appropriateness and accuracy Quality Level: High - Comprehensive indigenous knowledge analysis capability with emphasis on respect, relationship, and deference to indigenous leadership

docs.title: Indigenous Leader Analyst - Domain Validation Quiz
Purpose
docs.text: This quiz validates that the indigenous leader analyst applies indigenous knowledge systems correctly, honors traditional wisdom and sovereignty, and provides well-grounded analysis rooted in holistic worldviews, intergenerational time scales, and reciprocal relationships. Each scenario requires demonstration of cultural sensitivity, systems thinking from indigenous perspectives, and understanding of decolonization.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Sacred Site Protection vs. Renewable Energy Development
docs.text:
Event Description: A government approves a large-scale wind farm project on public lands that indigenous communities identify as sacred territory. The site contains burial grounds, ceremonial areas, and is part of traditional migration routes used for seasonal gathering practices spanning millennia. The wind farm promises 500 megawatts of clean energy, thousands of construction jobs, and significant tax revenue for economically depressed counties. Environmental impact assessments found no endangered species concerns and minimal habitat disruption. The indigenous nation was "consulted" through three public meetings but their concerns about spiritual significance, ceremonial disruption, and treaty violations were not incorporated into final plans. The nation argues this land was never legally ceded and remains sovereign territory under treaty law. The project also threatens viewsheds essential to ceremonial practices and would require roads fragmenting traditional gathering areas.

Analysis Task: Analyze this conflict through indigenous knowledge frameworks and sovereignty principles.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Worldview Clash Analysis:
  • Western: Land as resource, commodity, property to be developed
  • Indigenous: Land as sacred, ancestor, relative, living entity with rights
  • Western: Environmental impact = species count, habitat metrics
  • Indigenous: Impact = relationship disruption, spiritual harm, intergenerational obligation breach
  • Western: Linear time (immediate jobs/revenue)

  • Indigenous: Cyclical/intergenerational time (millennia of practice)

  • Sovereignty & Legal Framework:

  • Treaty rights: Legal standing, historical context, ongoing violations
  • Free, Prior, Informed Consent (FPIC - UN Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples)
  • Consultation vs. consent: "Consultation" as performative box-checking
  • Domestic dependent nations status: Legal limbo, sovereignty limitations
  • Sacred Sites Protection Act (inadequate enforcement)

  • Environmental racism: Marginalized lands targeted for industrial projects

  • Relational Ontology:

  • Land as kin, not property: Reciprocal obligations to care for relatives
  • Intergenerational responsibility: Seven generations principle
  • Ceremonial practice as essential (not recreational/cultural luxury)
  • Place-based knowledge: Cannot be relocated or substituted
  • Spiritual ecology: Non-material relationships with place

  • Burial grounds: Ancestors present, not merely historical artifacts

  • False Binary Critique:

  • Development vs. environment (both Western framings)
  • Jobs vs. culture (assumes economics trump spirituality)
  • Clean energy vs. indigenous rights (pits climate action against justice)

  • Alternatives ignored: Indigenous-led renewable development, different site selection, community benefit agreements with real sovereignty

  • Historical Context:

  • Pattern of dispossession: Land theft, forced removal, genocide
  • Resource extraction history: Mining, logging, dams on indigenous lands
  • Boarding schools, language loss, cultural genocide (ongoing trauma)
  • Environmental racism: Disproportionate toxic burden on indigenous communities

  • Contemporary: DAPL (Standing Rock), Line 3, lithium mining, etc.

  • Indigenous-Centered Solutions:

  • True consent: Project redesign or cancellation based on indigenous decision
  • Co-management: Joint governance with veto power for indigenous nation
  • Reparative justice: Land return, treaty enforcement
  • Indigenous-led renewable energy: On terms respecting sacred geography
  • Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) integration: Not extraction but partnership

  • Restorative practices: Healing harm already done

  • Decolonization Framework:

  • Land back movement: Return of stolen lands
  • Cognitive justice: Indigenous epistemologies as equally valid
  • Structural change: Not inclusion in extractive systems but transformation of systems
  • Self-determination: Indigenous nations deciding own futures
  • Relationship repair: Settler responsibility, accountability

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct application of indigenous knowledge systems, sovereignty principles, relational ontology
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of worldview analysis, historical context, structural critique
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear identification of power dynamics, alternative solutions, decolonial pathways
  • Historical/Contextual Grounding (0-10): References to treaty history, indigenous resistance, legal frameworks
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from indigenous perspectives to systemic analysis to solutions

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scenario 2: Traditional Ecological Knowledge and Climate Adaptation
docs.text:
Event Description: A coastal indigenous community faces accelerating climate impacts: Sea level rise threatening villages, warming waters depleting traditional fisheries, erosion destroying cultural sites, and changing seasonal patterns disrupting subsistence practices. Government agencies offer a managed retreat program (relocation to inland areas) and propose scientific climate adaptation research conducted by university teams. The indigenous community has millennia of Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) about environmental change, seasonal patterns, and adaptive practices. Elders share oral histories of previous climate shifts and adaptation strategies used by ancestors. The community wants to remain on ancestral lands and implement TEK-based adaptation but lacks funding and faces skepticism from government scientists who view TEK as "anecdotal." Meanwhile, universities want to "study" and "document" indigenous knowledge without offering partnership, benefit sharing, or recognition of intellectual sovereignty.

Analysis Task: Analyze this scenario through indigenous knowledge sovereignty and climate justice frameworks.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) - Nature & Value:
  • Multi-generational observational science (not anecdote)
  • Place-based, experiential, adaptive learning system
  • Holistic: Integrates ecological, spiritual, social dimensions
  • Oral transmission: Rich, precise, verified through practice
  • Complementary to Western science (not inferior/superior but different)

  • Predictive power: Long-term patterns, relationship changes

  • Knowledge Sovereignty & Intellectual Property:

  • TEK as intellectual and cultural property of indigenous peoples
  • Biopiracy history: Corporations/researchers extracting knowledge without consent/compensation
  • Research ethics: OCAP principles (Ownership, Control, Access, Possession)
  • Extractive research vs. partnership research
  • Who benefits from knowledge? Who has authority to share?

  • Indigenous data sovereignty: Self-determination over information

  • Epistemological Justice:

  • Western science as dominant/validated; TEK as "anecdotal/folkloric" (epistemic violence)
  • Double standards: Peer review for Western science, dismissal of intergenerational verification
  • Cognitive imperialism: One way of knowing imposed as universal
  • Two-Eyed Seeing (Etuaptmumk): Integrating TEK and Western science as equals

  • Indigenous scientists: Bridging worldviews, challenging hierarchies

  • Climate Justice & Indigenous Frontlines:

  • Indigenous peoples: 5% of population, protect 80% of biodiversity
  • Least responsibility for climate change, greatest impacts
  • Frontline communities: Arctic, small islands, coastal, forest-dependent
  • Climate colonialism: Solutions that displace indigenous peoples (conservation, mitigation projects)

  • Just transition: Must center indigenous rights and self-determination

  • Managed Retreat Critique:

  • Terminology: "Retreat" from whose perspective? (Defense of colonial state?)
  • Indigenous view: Ancestors, sacred sites, place-based identity cannot relocate
  • Forced displacement: Continuation of removal policies (Trail of Tears, Relocation Act)
  • Cultural genocide: Severing connection to land = destruction of identity

  • Alternatives: In-situ adaptation, land-based practices, flexible residence patterns

  • TEK-Based Adaptation Strategies:

  • Seasonal mobility: Traditional practice (not "retreat" but cyclical relationship)
  • Diversified subsistence: Multiple food sources, reduces vulnerability
  • Observation systems: Phenological indicators, animal behavior, plant signals
  • Adaptive management: Responding to change based on continuous relationship with place
  • Intergenerational resilience: Stories of past changes provide templates

  • Spiritual practice: Ceremonies for healing land, maintaining relationships

  • Partnership Framework (Not Extraction):

  • Co-production of knowledge: Equal partnership, mutual respect
  • Benefit sharing: Financial, recognition, capacity building
  • Community-led research: Indigenous nations set priorities, control process
  • Funding equity: Resources for indigenous-led adaptation
  • Long-term relationship: Not one-off study but ongoing collaboration
  • Protocol respect: Following indigenous governance around knowledge sharing

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct understanding of TEK, knowledge sovereignty, two-eyed seeing
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of epistemological, justice, partnership analysis
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear identification of extractive dynamics and authentic partnership models
  • Historical/Contextual Grounding (0-10): References to research ethics, indigenous science, climate justice
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from knowledge systems to justice to solutions

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scenario 3: Language Revitalization and Cultural Continuity
docs.text:
Event Description: An indigenous language spoken by only 47 fluent elders (all over age 70) faces imminent extinction. The language contains irreplaceable ecological knowledge, cultural concepts, and spiritual teachings that cannot be fully translated. The community has initiated a language revitalization program using immersion schools, elder-youth mentorship, and digital archiving. However, challenges are severe: Historical trauma from boarding schools (where children were punished for speaking indigenous languages) creates intergenerational pain around language use. Youth face pressure to prioritize English for economic opportunities. Linguists from universities offer to "preserve" the language through documentation but propose extractive methods (elders spend time with researchers rather than youth). Tech companies offer AI language learning apps but want to own the data and intellectual property. The community seeks a path that heals trauma, empowers youth, and keeps the language living (not just archived as artifact).

Analysis Task: Analyze language revitalization through indigenous cultural sovereignty and decolonization frameworks.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Language as Worldview:
  • Language = culture, epistemology, identity (not just communication tool)
  • Indigenous languages encode: Relationships to land, non-human kin, time, values
  • Concepts with no English equivalent: Entire categories of meaning
  • Grammar reflecting worldview: Animacy, verb-based vs. noun-based, relationality
  • Loss of language = loss of ways of knowing, being, relating

  • Example: Ecological terms describing plant relationships, seasonal indicators

  • Historical Trauma & Linguistic Genocide:

  • Boarding schools: "Kill the Indian, save the man" (linguistic and cultural genocide)
  • Punishment for speaking indigenous languages (physical abuse, humiliation)
  • Intergenerational trauma: Parents don't teach language to protect children
  • Internalized shame: Association of language with punishment, poverty, backwardness
  • Language shift: English as survival strategy under colonialism

  • Ongoing impacts: Fear, grief, disconnection around language

  • Living Language vs. Archive:

  • Living: Spoken in daily life, evolving, transmitting culture
  • Archived: Documentation (recordings, dictionaries) but no speakers
  • Risk: "Preservation" that prioritizes researchers over community use
  • False choice: Documentation can support revival if community-controlled
  • Reclamation: Language as resistance, healing, sovereignty act

  • Success measures: New speakers, language use domains, intergenerational transmission

  • Youth & Intergenerational Transmission:

  • Youth need: Reason to speak language (peers, contexts, cultural pride)
  • Elder knowledge: Fluency, cultural context, traditional teachings
  • Generation gap: Boarding school era broke transmission chain
  • Immersion programs: Most effective (total language environment)
  • Master-apprentice programs: One-on-one intensive, relationship-based

  • Land-based learning: Language taught through traditional practices on territory

  • Extractive Research Critique:

  • Linguists: Career advancement from indigenous languages, limited community benefit
  • Data extraction: Recordings, grammars published without community control
  • Time burden: Elders working with researchers instead of teaching youth
  • Ownership: Who controls recordings, materials, intellectual property?
  • Academic language: Documentation inaccessible to community members

  • Alternative: Community-based research, indigenous linguists, participatory methods

  • Technology & Intellectual Property:

  • Tech offers: AI apps, databases, digital tools (seem helpful)
  • IP concerns: Who owns data? Can corporation profit from indigenous language?
  • Data sovereignty: Indigenous control over language data, cultural protocols
  • Cultural appropriation risk: Sacred knowledge made publicly accessible
  • Useful tools: When community-owned, support (not replace) human transmission

  • Example: FirstVoices (community-controlled language archive)

  • Decolonial Language Revitalization:

  • Community-led: Indigenous governance over revitalization process
  • Healing-centered: Addresses trauma, creates safe spaces, rebuilds pride
  • Land-based: Language taught through relationship with territory
  • Intergenerational justice: Rebuilding transmission across generations
  • Resourced adequately: Funding for immersion schools, teacher training, elder honoraria
  • Political: Language rights, official status, education system integration
  • Cultural context: Language inseparable from ceremonies, stories, values

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct understanding of language-culture connection, historical trauma, revitalization methods
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of trauma analysis, extractive critique, decolonial frameworks
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear identification of living vs. archived language, community-led approaches
  • Historical/Contextual Grounding (0-10): References to boarding schools, language revitalization movements, indigenous linguistics
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from historical harm to healing-centered revitalization

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scenario 4: Resource Extraction and Free, Prior, Informed Consent (FPIC)
docs.text:
Event Description: A multinational corporation seeks to develop a lithium mine on lands adjacent to indigenous territory. Lithium is critical for electric vehicle batteries and clean energy transition. The government fast-tracks environmental approvals citing climate urgency. The mining project would: Consume massive water resources in arid region (threatening indigenous water sources), create tailings ponds with toxic contamination risk, require transportation infrastructure through indigenous lands, and operate for 30+ years. The corporation offers an "impact benefit agreement" with jobs, scholarships, and revenue sharing. However, the indigenous nation was not consulted before government approval, the benefit agreement is offered as a done deal (sign or project proceeds anyway), and the corporation conducts "community engagement" by meeting with individuals rather than respecting indigenous governance structures. The nation's legal and cultural decision-making process requires consensus, ceremonies, and multi-generational consideration, but the corporation demands a decision within 90 days.

Analysis Task: Analyze this scenario through FPIC principles, indigenous governance, and climate justice frameworks.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Free, Prior, Informed Consent (FPIC) - Principles:
  • Free: No coercion, intimidation, manipulation, or conditional offers
  • Prior: Before project approval/implementation, not after
  • Informed: Full information, time to analyze, culturally appropriate formats
  • Consent: Right to say no, not just "consultation" (veto power)
  • Legal basis: UN Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), ILO 169

  • Current case violations: Approval before consultation, timeline pressure, "sign or else" framing

  • Indigenous Governance & Decision-Making:

  • Collective process: Not individual sign-offs, community consensus
  • Cultural protocols: Ceremonies, elder councils, deliberation norms
  • Intergenerational consideration: Seven generations impact assessment
  • Spiritual dimension: Relationship with land, non-human relatives consulted
  • Timeline mismatch: Corporate quarterly vs. indigenous intergenerational

  • Respect for process: Settler obligation to follow indigenous governance, not impose timelines

  • Water as Relative & Life:

  • Indigenous water ontology: Water is alive, sacred, has rights
  • Water as first medicine: Spiritual and physical life
  • Watershed relationships: All beings dependent on water quality
  • Western approach: Water as resource to be extracted, commodified
  • Mining impacts: Depletion, contamination, intergenerational harm
  • Climate context: Arid regions, water scarcity intensifying

  • Water rights: Indigenous legal claims often senior to mining claims

  • False Climate Solution Critique:

  • "Green sacrifice zones": Indigenous lands targeted for "clean" energy minerals
  • Climate colonialism: Solutions that harm frontline communities
  • Extraction continuity: Lithium mining replicates colonial resource extraction
  • Alternatives exist: Battery recycling, alternative chemistries, reduced consumption
  • Just transition: Must not repeat extraction patterns under green label

  • Indigenous climate leadership: Most effective land stewards (should lead, not sacrifice)

  • Impact Benefit Agreement (IBA) Critique:

  • Offered post-approval: Not FPIC, but mitigation after violation
  • Economic coercion: Jobs/money to overcome opposition
  • Individual vs. collective: Divides community, undermines governance
  • Inadequate: Money can't compensate for water contamination, sacred site destruction
  • Liability limits: Corporations insulate from long-term harm

  • Alternative: Indigenous nations as economic partners with equity, veto power, co-management

  • Intergenerational Justice:

  • 30-year mine, multi-century impacts (tailings, water, reclamation failure)
  • Seven generations principle: Consider 7 generations forward
  • Irreversible harm: Water contamination, ecosystem disruption
  • Ancestors and descendants: Both present in decision-making
  • Precautionary principle: When harm uncertain, protect

  • Reciprocal obligation: Current generation as caretakers, not owners

  • Indigenous-Centered Alternatives:

  • No means no: Respect consent refusal
  • Redesign: Different location, indigenous-led site selection
  • Indigenous equity: Nation as co-owner, not "beneficiary"
  • Co-governance: Joint management with indigenous veto power
  • Circular economy: Prioritize recycling, reduce extraction demand
  • Land back: Return lands to indigenous management for protection
  • Legal enforcement: Strengthen FPIC with domestic enforcement mechanisms

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct understanding of FPIC, indigenous governance, relational ontology
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of consent analysis, power dynamics, alternatives
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear identification of violations, false solutions, decolonial pathways
  • Historical/Contextual Grounding (0-10): References to UNDRIP, extraction history, climate justice
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from FPIC principles to structural critique to solutions

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scenario 5: Urban Indigenous Identity and Visibility
docs.text:
Event Description: A major city with a large but largely invisible urban indigenous population (60% of indigenous people in the country live in cities) undertakes an initiative to "recognize and celebrate" indigenous heritage. Proposals include: Renaming streets after indigenous leaders, installing public art by indigenous artists, land acknowledgment statements at government events, and indigenous cultural center. However, no consultation occurred with urban indigenous community organizations before announcing these plans. The initiatives are performative (symbolic gestures without structural change). Meanwhile, urban indigenous communities face: Homelessness crisis disproportionately affecting indigenous people, over-representation in incarceration, child welfare system apprehension of indigenous children, lack of culturally appropriate services, racism in housing/employment, and disconnection from land-based practices. Indigenous community leaders say: "We don't need land acknowledgments, we need land back. We don't need art, we need housing. We don't need symbolic gestures, we need sovereignty and resources."

Analysis Task: Analyze this scenario through decolonization, urban indigenous experience, and structural change frameworks.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Urban Indigenous Experience - Complexity:
  • Displacement: Many urban indigenous people result from forced relocation policies
  • Diaspora: Separated from home territories, traditional governance, language
  • Resilience: Urban indigenous communities create new forms of kinship, culture
  • Diversity: Multiple nations, intertribal connections, varied colonial impacts
  • Invisibility: Erasure narrative (indigenous people as historical/rural only)

  • Dual consciousness: Maintaining connection to home territories while navigating urban life

  • Symbolic Reconciliation Critique:

  • Land acknowledgments: Empty ritual without land return or material change
  • Performative inclusion: Indigenous imagery/art while structure remains colonial
  • Diversity washing: Appearance of progress masking ongoing harm
  • Settler comfort: Gestures that make settlers feel good without accountability
  • Indigenous labor: Expected to provide cultural education, ceremonies for settler consumption

  • "Reconciliation" vs. decolonization: Reconciliation maintains status quo, decolonization transforms power

  • Structural vs. Symbolic Change:

  • Symbolic: Acknowledgments, art, celebrations, apologies
  • Structural: Housing, sovereignty, resources, legal reform, land return
  • Current scenario: All symbolic, zero structural
  • What's needed: Transfer of resources, power, land

  • Adequate consultation: Would have revealed community priorities (housing, not statues)

  • Urban Indigenous Issues - Systemic:

  • Housing: Homelessness crisis, discrimination, displacement, gentrification
  • Child welfare: Continued apprehension (Sixties Scoop ongoing), cultural genocide
  • Incarceration: Over-representation, criminalization of poverty/trauma
  • Healthcare: Lack of culturally safe services, racism, worse outcomes
  • Education: Dropout rates, curriculum erasure, hostile environments
  • Economic: Employment discrimination, poverty, lack of opportunities

  • Root cause: All connected to colonialism, ongoing dispossession

  • Decolonization - What It Requires:

  • Land back: Return of stolen lands (not just acknowledgment they were stolen)
  • Resource redistribution: Reparations, funding for indigenous-led services
  • Sovereignty: Self-determination, indigenous governance authority
  • Legal reform: Jurisdiction, child welfare, policing, justice systems
  • Structural transformation: Not inclusion in oppressive systems but new systems
  • Settler accountability: Bearing costs of change, confronting complicity

  • Indigenous leadership: Not consultation but decision-making power

  • Urban Indigenous Leadership & Solutions:

  • Indigenous-led housing (not shelters but culturally grounded homes)
  • Indigenous child welfare jurisdiction (keeping families together)
  • Urban reserves (land base within cities for indigenous sovereignty)
  • Indigenous cultural centers with wraparound services (not just museums)
  • Funding self-determination (core funding for indigenous organizations)
  • Land-based healing programs (access to traditional territories)

  • Indigenous urbanism: Cities designed with indigenous values, governance

  • Consultation vs. Consent:

  • True consultation: Before decisions, with power to shape outcomes
  • Current case: Announced first, community reaction after
  • FPIC application: Applies to urban policy affecting indigenous people
  • Indigenous governance: Urban indigenous organizations as authorities
  • Co-design: Indigenous communities lead initiative design
  • Accountability: Ongoing relationship, not one-time event

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct understanding of urban indigenous experience, decolonization vs. reconciliation
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of structural analysis, symbolic vs. material critique
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear identification of performative gestures and structural alternatives
  • Historical/Contextual Grounding (0-10): References to relocation policies, urban indigenous movements
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from settler colonialism to structural change requirements

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scoring Summary
docs.text: Scenario Max Score Passing Score 1. Sacred Site Protection 50 35 2. Traditional Ecological Knowledge 50 35 3. Language Revitalization 50 35 4. FPIC and Resource Extraction 50 35 5. Urban Indigenous Identity 50 35 Total 250 175

docs.title: Passing Criteria
docs.text:
To demonstrate indigenous leader analyst competence:

  • Minimum per scenario: 35/50 (70%)
  • Overall minimum: 175/250 (70%)
  • Must pass at least 4 of 5 scenarios

docs.title: Evaluation Dimensions
docs.text:
Each scenario is scored on:

  1. Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct application of indigenous knowledge systems, sovereignty principles, decolonization frameworks
  2. Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of worldview analysis, structural critique, historical context
  3. Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear identification of power dynamics, colonial continuities, indigenous-centered solutions
  4. Historical/Contextual Grounding (0-10): Use of treaty history, indigenous resistance, decolonial movements
  5. Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from indigenous perspectives to systemic analysis to transformative solutions

docs.title: What High-Quality Indigenous-Centered Analysis Looks Like
docs.text:
Excellent (45-50 points):

  • Centers indigenous worldviews, epistemologies, and governance systems
  • Demonstrates sophisticated understanding of settler colonialism as ongoing structure
  • Applies decolonization frameworks (not just inclusion/diversity)
  • Honors indigenous sovereignty and self-determination
  • Recognizes diversity among indigenous peoples while identifying shared colonial patterns
  • Analyzes power dynamics and structural violence with clarity
  • Proposes solutions that transform (not reform) colonial systems
  • Shows humility about limits of non-indigenous analysis
  • Integrates historical context with contemporary resistance movements
  • Acknowledges intergenerational and relational dimensions

Good (35-44 points):

  • Correctly identifies key indigenous perspectives and sovereignty issues
  • Understands distinction between symbolic and structural change
  • Recognizes historical trauma and ongoing colonialism
  • Applies relevant frameworks (FPIC, UNDRIP, TEK, etc.)
  • Proposes solutions that center indigenous leadership
  • Demonstrates cultural sensitivity and respect

Needs Improvement (<35 points):

  • Centers settler perspectives or treats indigenous views as one among many
  • Conflates diversity/inclusion with decolonization
  • Treats indigenous knowledge as inferior or merely cultural (not epistemological)
  • Ignores sovereignty and self-determination
  • Proposes solutions that don't challenge colonial structures
  • Lacks historical context or treats colonialism as past
  • Stereotypes or essentializes indigenous peoples
  • Extractive approach (using indigenous knowledge without respecting protocols)
  • Superficial "both sides" framing that obscures power imbalances

docs.title: For Self-Assessment
docs.text:
1. Attempt each scenario analysis
  2. Center indigenous perspectives and sovereignty
  3. Apply decolonization frameworks
  4. Compare your analysis to expected elements
  5. Score yourself honestly on each dimension
  6. Identify areas for deeper learning (with humility and respect for indigenous knowledge sovereignty)

docs.title: For Automated Testing (Claude Agent SDK)
docs.text:
from claude_agent_sdk import Agent, TestHarness

agent = Agent.load("indigenous-leader-analyst")
quiz = load_quiz_scenarios("tests/quiz.md")

results = []
for scenario in quiz.scenarios:
    analysis = agent.analyze(scenario.event)
    score = evaluate_analysis(analysis, scenario.expected_elements)
    results.append({"scenario": scenario.name, "score": score})

assert sum(r["score"] for r in results) >= 175  # Overall passing
assert sum(1 for r in results if r["score"] >= 35) >= 4  # At least 4 scenarios pass

docs.title: For Continuous Improvement
docs.text:
• Add new scenarios as decolonization movements evolve
  • Update expected elements in consultation with indigenous scholars and leaders
  • Refine scoring criteria based on indigenous-centered analysis standards
  • Use failures to improve indigenous leader analyst skill (with cultural humility)

docs.title: Important Notes on Using This Skill
docs.text:
• Positionality: Acknowledge your relationship to settler colonialism and indigenous peoples
  • Humility: Non-indigenous people should approach this work with humility, recognizing limits
  • Learning: This is a starting point, not comprehensive indigenous knowledge
  • Relationships: Authentic solidarity requires relationship-building, not just analytical skill
  • Action: Analysis must lead to material support for indigenous sovereignty and decolonization

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This skill provides a systematic 6-phase workflow for investigating and understanding existing systems, codebases, and architectures. Unlike development workflows optimized for implementation, this workflow is optimized for exploration, understanding, and knowledge capture.

docs.title: When to Use This Skill
docs.text:
Investigation Tasks (use this workflow):

  • "Investigate how the authentication system works"
  • "Explain the neo4j memory integration"
  • "Understand why CI is failing consistently"
  • "Analyze the reflection system architecture"
  • "Research what hooks are triggered during session start"

Development Tasks (use DEFAULT_WORKFLOW.md instead):

  • "Implement OAuth support"
  • "Build a new API endpoint"
  • "Add feature X"
  • "Fix bug Y"

docs.title: Core Philosophy
docs.text: Exploration First: Define scope and strategy before diving into code Parallel Deep Dives: Deploy multiple agents simultaneously for efficient information gathering Verification Required: Test understanding through practical application Knowledge Capture: Document findings to prevent repeat investigations

docs.title: Phase 1: Scope Definition
docs.text:
Purpose: Define investigation boundaries and success criteria before any exploration.

Tasks:

  • FIRST: Identify explicit user requirements - What specific questions must be answered?
  • Use prompt-writer agent to clarify investigation scope
  • Use ambiguity agent if questions are unclear
  • Define what counts as "understanding achieved"
  • List specific questions that must be answered
  • Set boundaries: What's in scope vs. out of scope
  • Estimate investigation depth needed (surface-level vs. deep dive)

Success Criteria:

  • Clear list of questions to answer
  • Defined scope boundaries
  • Measurable success criteria (e.g., "can explain system flow", "can diagram architecture")

Deliverables:

  • Investigation scope document with:
  • Core questions to answer
  • Success criteria
  • Scope boundaries (what's included/excluded)
  • Estimated depth and timeline

docs.title: Phase 2: Exploration Strategy
docs.text:
Purpose: Plan which agents to deploy and what to investigate, preventing inefficient random exploration.

Tasks:

  • Use architect agent to design exploration strategy
  • Use patterns agent to check for similar past investigations
  • Identify key areas to explore (code paths, configurations, documentation)
  • Select specialized agents for parallel deployment in Phase 3
  • Create investigation roadmap with priorities
  • Identify potential dead ends to avoid
  • Plan verification approach (how to test understanding)

Agent Selection Guidelines:

  • For code understanding: analyzer, patterns agents
  • For system architecture: architect, api-designer agents
  • For performance issues: optimizer, analyzer agents
  • For security concerns: security, patterns agents
  • For integration flows: integration, database agents

Success Criteria:

  • Clear exploration roadmap
  • List of agents to deploy in Phase 3
  • Prioritized investigation areas

Deliverables:

  • Exploration strategy document with:
  • Investigation roadmap
  • Agent deployment plan for Phase 3
  • Priority order for exploration
  • Expected outputs from each exploration

docs.title: Phase 3: Parallel Deep Dives
docs.text:
Purpose: Deploy multiple exploration agents simultaneously to gather information efficiently.

CRITICAL: This phase uses PARALLEL EXECUTION by default.

Tasks:

  • Deploy selected agents in PARALLEL based on Phase 2 strategy
  • Common parallel patterns:
  • [analyzer(module1), analyzer(module2), analyzer(module3)] - Multiple code areas
  • [analyzer, patterns, security] - Multiple perspectives on same area
  • [architect, database, integration] - System architecture exploration
  • Each agent explores their assigned area independently
  • Collect findings from all parallel explorations
  • Identify connections and dependencies between findings
  • Note any unexpected discoveries or anomalies

Parallel Agent Examples:

Investigation: "How does the reflection system work?"
→ [analyzer(~/.amplihack/.claude/tools/amplihack/hooks/), patterns(reflection), integration(logging)]

Investigation: "Why is CI failing?"
→ [analyzer(ci-config), patterns(ci-failures), integration(github-actions)]

Investigation: "Understand authentication flow"
→ [analyzer(auth-module), security(auth), patterns(auth), integration(external-auth)]

Success Criteria:

  • All planned agents deployed and completed
  • Findings from each exploration collected
  • Connections between findings identified

Deliverables:

  • Findings report with:
  • Summary from each parallel exploration
  • Code paths and flow diagrams
  • Architectural insights
  • Unexpected discoveries
  • Open questions for verification

docs.title: Phase 4: Verification & Testing
docs.text:
Purpose: Test and validate understanding through practical application.

Tasks:

  • Create hypotheses based on Phase 3 findings
  • Design practical tests to verify understanding:
  • Trace specific code paths manually
  • Examine logs and outputs
  • Test edge cases and assumptions
  • Verify configuration effects
  • Run verification tests
  • Document what was tested and results
  • Identify gaps in understanding
  • Refine hypotheses based on test results
  • Repeat verification for any unclear areas

Verification Examples:

Understanding: "Authentication uses JWT tokens"
Verification: Trace actual token creation and validation in code

Understanding: "CI fails because of dependency conflict"
Verification: Check CI logs, reproduce locally, verify fix works

Understanding: "Reflection analyzes all user messages"
Verification: Examine reflection logs, trace message processing

Success Criteria:

  • All hypotheses tested
  • Understanding verified through practical tests
  • Gaps in understanding identified and filled

Deliverables:

  • Verification report with:
  • Tests performed
  • Results and observations
  • Confirmed understanding
  • Remaining gaps or uncertainties

docs.title: Phase 5: Synthesis
docs.text:
Purpose: Compile findings into coherent explanation that answers original questions.

Tasks:

  • Use reviewer agent to check completeness of findings
  • Use patterns agent to identify reusable patterns discovered
  • Synthesize findings from Phases 3-4 into coherent explanation
  • Create visual artifacts (diagrams, flow charts) if helpful
  • Answer each question from Phase 1 scope definition
  • Identify what worked well vs. what was unexpected
  • Note any assumptions or uncertainties remaining
  • Prepare clear explanation suitable for user

Synthesis Outputs:

  1. Executive Summary: 2-3 sentence answer to main question
  2. Detailed Explanation: Complete explanation with supporting evidence
  3. Visual Aids: Diagrams showing system flow, architecture, etc.
  4. Key Insights: Non-obvious discoveries or patterns
  5. Remaining Unknowns: What's still unclear or uncertain

Success Criteria:

  • All Phase 1 questions answered
  • Explanation is clear and complete
  • Findings supported by evidence from verification
  • Visual aids clarify complex areas

Deliverables:

  • Investigation report with all 5 synthesis outputs
  • Ready for knowledge capture in Phase 6

docs.title: Phase 6: Knowledge Capture
docs.text:
Purpose: Create durable documentation so this investigation never needs to be repeated.

Tasks:

  • Update .claude/context/DISCOVERIES.md with key insights
  • Update .claude/context/PATTERNS.md if reusable patterns found
  • Create or update relevant documentation files
  • Add inline code comments for critical understanding
  • Optional: Create GitHub issue for follow-up improvements
  • Optional: Update architecture diagrams if needed
  • Ensure future investigators can find this knowledge easily

Documentation Guidelines:

## Discovery: [Brief Title]

**Context**: What was investigated and why
**Key Findings**:

- Main insight 1
- Main insight 2
  - **Supporting Evidence**: Links to code, logs, or verification tests
  - **Implications**: How this affects the project
  - **Related Patterns**: Links to similar patterns in PATTERNS.md

Success Criteria:

  • DISCOVERIES.md updated with investigation results
  • Relevant documentation files updated
  • Knowledge is discoverable by future investigators
  • No information loss

Deliverables:

  • Updated DISCOVERIES.md
  • Updated PATTERNS.md (if applicable)
  • Updated project documentation
  • Optional: GitHub issues for improvements
  • Investigation session log in ~/.amplihack/.claude/runtime/logs/

docs.title: Transitioning to Development Workflow
docs.text:
After investigation completes, if the task requires implementation (not just understanding), transition to DEFAULT_WORKFLOW.md:

  1. Resume at Step 4 (Research and Design) with the knowledge gained from investigation
  2. Or resume at Step 5 (Implement the Solution) if the investigation already provided clear design guidance
  3. Use investigation findings from DISCOVERIES.md and session logs to inform design decisions

Example Hybrid Workflow:

User: "/ultrathink investigate how authentication works, then add OAuth support"

Phase 1: Investigation
→ Run INVESTIGATION_WORKFLOW.md (6 phases)
→ Complete understanding of existing auth system
→ Document findings in DISCOVERIES.md

Phase 2: Development
→ Transition to DEFAULT_WORKFLOW.md
→ Resume at Step 4 (Research and Design)
→ Use investigation insights to design OAuth integration
→ Continue through Step 15 (implementation → testing → PR)

When to Transition:

  • Investigation reveals implementation is needed
  • User explicitly requested both investigation + development
  • Follow-up work identified during knowledge capture

docs.title: Efficiency Targets
docs.text:
Target Efficiency: This workflow targets a 30-40% reduction in message count compared to ad-hoc investigation.

Ad-Hoc Approach Investigation Workflow 70-90 messages 40-60 messages Frequent backtracking Planned exploration Redundant investigation Parallel deep dives Unclear scope Explicit scope definition Lost knowledge Documented insights

Efficiency Gains Come From:

  1. Scope Definition prevents scope creep and wandering
  2. Exploration Strategy prevents random unproductive exploration
  3. Parallel Deep Dives maximize information gathering speed
  4. Verification Phase catches misunderstandings early
  5. Synthesis ensures all questions answered
  6. Knowledge Capture prevents repeat investigations

docs.title: Similarities (Structural Consistency)
docs.text:
Both workflows share core principles:

  • Explicit phases with clear deliverables
  • Agent-driven execution at each phase
  • Quality gates preventing premature progression
  • Knowledge capture and documentation
  • TodoWrite tracking for progress management

docs.title: Differences (Investigation vs. Development)
docs.text: Aspect Investigation Workflow DEFAULT_WORKFLOW.md Goal Understanding Implementation Phases 6 phases Multi-step workflow Execution Exploration-first Implementation-first Parallel Focus Phase 3 (Deep Dives) Various steps Testing Understanding verification Code validation Deliverable Documentation Working code Git Usage Optional Required (branches, PRs)

docs.title: Phase Mapping (For User Familiarity)
docs.text: Investigation Phase DEFAULT_WORKFLOW Equivalent Purpose Phase 1: Scope Definition Step 1: Requirements Clarification Define what success looks like Phase 2: Exploration Strategy Step 4: Research and Design Plan the approach Phase 3: Parallel Deep Dives Step 5: Implementation Execute the plan (explore vs. build) Phase 4: Verification Steps 7-8: Testing Validate results Phase 5: Synthesis Step 11: Review Ensure quality and completeness Phase 6: Knowledge Capture Step 15: Cleanup Make results durable

docs.title: Integration with UltraThink
docs.text:
UltraThink Workflow Detection: When /ultrathink is invoked, it automatically detects investigation tasks using keywords and suggests this workflow.

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
To customize this workflow:

  1. Edit ~/.amplihack/.claude/workflow/INVESTIGATION_WORKFLOW.md to modify, add, or remove phases
  2. Adjust agent deployment strategies for your needs
  3. Add project-specific investigation patterns
  4. Update efficiency targets based on your metrics

Changes take effect immediately for future investigations.

docs.title: Success Metrics
docs.text:
Track these metrics to validate workflow effectiveness:

  • Message Count: Target 30-40% reduction vs. ad-hoc (to be validated)
  • Investigation Time: Track time to completion
  • Knowledge Reuse: How often DISCOVERIES.md prevents repeat work
  • Completeness: Percentage of investigations with full documentation
  • User Satisfaction: Clear understanding achieved

docs.title: Key Principles
docs.text:
• Scope first, explore second - Define boundaries before diving in
  • Parallel exploration is key - Deploy multiple agents simultaneously in Phase 3
  • Verify understanding - Test your hypotheses in Phase 4
  • Capture knowledge - Always update DISCOVERIES.md in Phase 6
  • This workflow optimizes for understanding, not implementation

When in doubt about investigation vs. development:

  • Investigation: "I need to understand X"
  • Development: "I need to build/fix/implement X"

docs.title: Journalist Analyst Skill
docs.text: Analyze events through the lens of journalism, applying the 5 Ws and H, investigative methods, and fact-checking to verify truth and serve public interest.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Journalist Analyst skill enables Claude to perform rigorous journalistic analysis of events, applying established reporting frameworks, source evaluation techniques, and ethical journalism principles. Drawing on professional standards and investigative methods, this skill provides insights into:

  • Factual Foundation: The 5 Ws and H (Who, What, When, Where, Why, How)
  • Source Credibility: Evaluating reliability, bias, and proximity to events
  • Information Gaps: What's missing, what needs verification
  • Newsworthiness: Timeliness, impact, proximity, prominence, conflict
  • Framing and Bias: How stories are told, what's emphasized or omitted
  • Ethical Dimensions: Truth-seeking, minimizing harm, independence, accountability

docs.title: What Makes This Different
docs.text:
Unlike general analysis, journalist analysis:

  1. Focuses on Verification: Always asks "How do we know this is true?"
  2. Applies Systematic Frameworks: 5 Ws and H, inverted pyramid, sourcing standards
  3. Evaluates Sources Rigorously: Credibility, proximity, bias, corroboration
  4. Identifies Information Gaps: What's missing, what questions remain
  5. Serves Public Interest: What citizens need to know, accountability
  6. Grounds in Facts: Distinguishes fact, opinion, and analysis clearly

docs.title: Breaking News Analysis
docs.text:
• Rapidly assessing developing events
  • Verifying emerging claims
  • Identifying what's known vs. unknown
  • Evaluating initial reporting quality

docs.title: Fact-Checking
docs.text:
• Verifying specific claims
  • Identifying misinformation
  • Assessing evidence quality
  • Tracking claims to original sources

docs.title: Source Evaluation
docs.text:
• Assessing credibility and reliability
  • Identifying bias and conflicts of interest
  • Evaluating expert qualifications
  • Determining source proximity to events

docs.title: Media Criticism
docs.text:
• Analyzing how news is framed
  • Identifying what's emphasized or omitted
  • Comparing coverage across outlets
  • Recognizing bias patterns

docs.title: Core Frameworks
docs.text:
• 5 Ws and H: Who, What, When, Where, Why, How - complete story elements
  • Inverted Pyramid: Most important information first, decreasing priority
  • Newsworthiness Criteria: Timeliness, proximity, impact, prominence, conflict, human interest, novelty
  • Source Evaluation: Authority, proximity, bias, corroboration, transparency

docs.title: Ethical Principles (SPJ Code)
docs.text:
• Seek Truth and Report It: Verify, provide context, acknowledge mistakes
  • Minimize Harm: Balance public need vs. potential harm, show compassion
  • Act Independently: Avoid conflicts, resist pressure, distinguish news from opinion
  • Be Accountable: Explain choices, respond to questions, correct errors promptly

docs.title: Investigative Methods
docs.text:
• Document Analysis: Public records, financial disclosures, FOIA requests
  • Following the Money: Financial relationships, conflicts of interest
  • Data Journalism: Statistical analysis, pattern recognition, visualization
  • Human Sources: Whistleblowers, insiders, experts, affected parties

docs.title: Verification Techniques
docs.text:
• Identify Claims: What needs checking
  • Find Original Source: Trace to primary sources
  • Seek Corroboration: Multiple independent sources
  • Check Context: Are statistics used appropriately?
  • Assess Confidence: Verified, likely, uncertain, false

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Claude, use the journalist-analyst skill to analyze [EVENT/CLAIM/STORY].

Examples:
- "Use journalist-analyst to fact-check this policy announcement."
- "Analyze the breaking news story using journalist-analyst skill."
- "Use the journalist skill to evaluate the credibility of these sources."

docs.title: Advanced Usage
docs.text:
Specify particular frameworks or focus areas:

"Use journalist-analyst to answer the 5 Ws and H for this event."

"Apply journalist-analyst to compare how different outlets are framing this story."

"Use journalist-analyst to identify information gaps and follow-up questions."

docs.title: Analysis Process
docs.text:
The journalist analyst follows a systematic 10-step process:

  1. Establish Basic Facts (5 Ws and H) - Systematically answer foundational questions
  2. Evaluate Sources - Assess credibility, proximity, bias, adequacy
  3. Assess Newsworthiness - Apply criteria, determine significance
  4. Identify Information Gaps - Note missing Ws, unchallenged claims, absent perspectives
  5. Analyze Framing - Examine how story is presented, what's emphasized
  6. Verify Key Claims - Seek independent verification, check against original sources
  7. Provide Context - Historical background, comparative analysis, perspective
  8. Assess Ethical Dimensions - Consider harm vs. public interest, fairness, transparency
  9. Construct Timeline - Build chronology, identify cause-effect relationships
  10. Synthesize Findings - Integrate analysis, acknowledge uncertainty, recommend follow-up

docs.title: Example 1: Policy Announcement
docs.text:
Event: Government announces $500B stimulus package

Journalistic Analysis:

  • Who: Government officials, affected industries, taxpayers
  • What: $500B stimulus (breakdown needed)
  • When: Announced today (implementation timeline?)
  • Where: National (distribution?)
  • Why: Combat recession (economic indicators?)
  • How: Tax cuts, direct payments, infrastructure (details?)

Source Evaluation: Official government source (authoritative but interested party), need independent expert verification

Information Gaps: Exact allocation, funding mechanism, economic impact projections, political feasibility

Newsworthiness: High - timely, significant impact, major policy

Follow-Up: Verify figures, consult independent economists, interview affected groups, check legislative process

docs.title: Example 2: Corporate Scandal
docs.text:
Event: Tech company accused of deceptive data collection

Journalistic Analysis:

  • Verification Strategy: Obtain internal documents, analyze code, consult independent experts, interview employees
  • Source Assessment: Whistleblower + documentary evidence + independent verification = strong
  • Information Gaps: Exact users affected, company response, regulatory action, user protection steps
  • Ethical Dimensions: Clear public interest, protect whistleblower, don't expose individual user data, give company fair chance to respond

Investigation Path: Documentary evidence → expert verification → company response → comprehensive report → ongoing coverage

docs.title: Example 3: Comparing Coverage
docs.text:
Event: Protest covered differently by two outlets

Analysis:

  • Outlet A: Headline emphasizes disruption, sources business owners/police, language "mob/chaos," omits protest rationale
  • Outlet B: Headline emphasizes turnout/message, sources organizers/participants, language "activists/demonstrators," omits disruption impacts
  • Both: Selective sourcing, biased framing, violations of balance standards
  • Implication: Audiences consuming only one outlet get distorted picture, media literacy essential

docs.title: Quality Standards
docs.text:
A complete journalist analysis includes:

✓ 5 Ws and H Answered: Complete factual foundation ✓ Source Evaluation: Credibility assessed, bias noted ✓ Verification: Key claims checked, confidence levels stated ✓ Information Gaps Identified: What's missing, what follow-up needed ✓ Context Provided: Background, historical precedents, perspective ✓ Newsworthiness Assessed: Significance and public interest evaluated ✓ Framing Analyzed: How story is told, what's emphasized/omitted ✓ Ethics Considered: Balance, harm, fairness, transparency ✓ Multiple Perspectives: Diverse sources, varied viewpoints ✓ Fact vs. Opinion: Clear distinctions maintained

docs.title: Professional Organizations
docs.text:
• SPJ (Society of Professional Journalists): https://www.spj.org/
  • SPJ Code of Ethics: Industry standard for ethical journalism
  • IRE (Investigative Reporters and Editors): https://www.ire.org/
  • Poynter Institute: https://www.poynter.org/

docs.title: Fact-Checking
docs.text:
• PolitiFact: https://www.politifact.com/
  • FactCheck.org: https://www.factcheck.org/
  • Snopes: https://www.snopes.com/

docs.text:
• AP Stylebook: Industry standard for journalism style
  • Reuters Handbook of Journalism: Principles and practices
  • Verification Handbook: Digital age verification techniques

docs.title: When should I use journalist-analyst vs. other analysts?
docs.text:
Use journalist-analyst when focus is:

  • Fact verification and truth-seeking
  • Source evaluation and credibility
  • Information gathering and completeness
  • Breaking news and rapid assessment
  • Media analysis and bias detection
  • Public accountability and transparency

Use other analysts when focus is:

  • Economic impacts → Economist
  • Political power dynamics → Political Scientist
  • Historical context → Historian
  • Narrative structure → Novelist

docs.title: Can journalist analysis be combined with other perspectives?
docs.text:
Absolutely! Journalistic analysis is particularly powerful when combined with:

  • Economist: Verifies economic claims, provides data context
  • Political Scientist: Verifies political claims, institutional analysis
  • Historian: Provides historical context and precedents
  • Poet: Analyzes language, rhetoric, emotional impact

docs.title: What if sources conflict?
docs.text:
When sources disagree:

  1. Assess relative credibility of each source
  2. Look for additional corroboration
  3. Present multiple perspectives clearly
  4. Acknowledge uncertainty
  5. Identify what additional evidence would help
  6. Distinguish between factual disagreements and opinion differences

docs.title: Integration with Other Skills
docs.text:
Journalist analysis complements:

  • Decision Logger: Document verification decisions and sourcing
  • Philosophy Guardian: Ensure analysis follows ruthless simplicity
  • Fact-Checking Tools: Integrate with verification resources
  • Knowledge Extractor: Capture patterns in misinformation

This skill improves through use. Share feedback on:

  • What verification techniques worked well
  • What sources were most helpful
  • What patterns emerged in bias or framing
  • What additional frameworks would be valuable
