docs.text:
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)

docs.title: Extract Tables
docs.text:
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:

docs.title: Advanced Table Extraction
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)

docs.title: Basic PDF Creation
docs.text:
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()

docs.title: Create PDF with Multiple Pages
docs.text:
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)

docs.title: Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
docs.text:
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)

docs.title: Add Watermark
docs.text:
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)

docs.title: Password Protection
docs.text:
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password

docs.text: This document provides practical examples of using the PDF skill in Claude Code conversations. These examples demonstrate common workflows and expected outcomes.

docs.title: Example 1: Extract Text from a Research Paper
Scenario
docs.text: You have a research paper PDF and need to extract all text for analysis.

docs.title: Conversation
docs.text:
User: Extract all text from research_paper.pdf and save it to a text file

Claude: I'll extract the text from the PDF using pdfplumber for better layout preservation.

import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("research_paper.pdf") as pdf:
    text = ""
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text += page.extract_text()
        text += "\n\n--- Page Break ---\n\n"

with open("research_paper_text.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(text)

print(f"Extracted text from {len(pdf.pages)} pages")

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
• research_paper_text.txt file created with all extracted text
  • Text preserves paragraph structure and layout
  • Page breaks clearly marked

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: You have a financial report PDF with multiple tables that need to be extracted and analyzed in Excel.

docs.title: Conversation
docs.text:
User: Extract all tables from financial_report.pdf and save them to Excel

Claude: I'll use pdfplumber to extract tables and pandas to create a structured Excel file.

import pdfplumber
import pandas as pd

all_tables = []

with pdfplumber.open("financial_report.pdf") as pdf:
    for page_num, page in enumerate(pdf.pages, 1):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table_num, table in enumerate(tables, 1):
            if table and len(table) > 1:
                # First row as headers
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                df['source_page'] = page_num
                df['table_number'] = table_num
                all_tables.append(df)

if all_tables:
    # Save each table to separate sheet
    with pd.ExcelWriter("financial_tables.xlsx", engine='openpyxl') as writer:
        for i, df in enumerate(all_tables, 1):
            sheet_name = f"Table_{i}_Page_{df['source_page'].iloc[0]}"
            df.drop(['source_page', 'table_number'], axis=1).to_excel(
                writer, sheet_name=sheet_name, index=False
            )

    print(f"Extracted {len(all_tables)} tables to financial_tables.xlsx")
else:
    print("No tables found in PDF")

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
• financial_tables.xlsx file with multiple sheets
  • Each sheet contains one extracted table
  • Sheet names indicate source page
  • Headers preserved from PDF

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Generate a multi-page report PDF with title, sections, and formatted text.

docs.title: Conversation
docs.text:
User: Create a sales report PDF with title "Q4 2024 Sales Report", three sections, and a summary table

Claude: I'll use reportlab to create a structured PDF with proper formatting.

from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet
from reportlab.lib.units import inch
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, Table, TableStyle, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib import colors

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("Q4_2024_Sales_Report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Title
title = Paragraph("Q4 2024 Sales Report", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 0.5*inch))

# Executive Summary
story.append(Paragraph("Executive Summary", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph(
    "Total sales increased 15% compared to Q3 2024, driven by strong performance "
    "in the enterprise segment. Key highlights include...",
    styles['Normal']
))
story.append(Spacer(1, 0.3*inch))

# Section 1: Revenue Breakdown
story.append(Paragraph("Revenue Breakdown", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph(
    "Revenue distribution across segments showed significant growth...",
    styles['Normal']
))
story.append(Spacer(1, 0.2*inch))

# Summary Table
data = [
    ['Segment', 'Q3 2024', 'Q4 2024', 'Growth'],
    ['Enterprise', '$2.5M', '$3.1M', '24%'],
    ['SMB', '$1.8M', '$2.0M', '11%'],
    ['Consumer', '$0.9M', '$1.0M', '11%'],
    ['Total', '$5.2M', '$6.1M', '17%']
]

table = Table(data, colWidths=[2*inch, 1.5*inch, 1.5*inch, 1*inch])
table.setStyle(TableStyle([
    ('BACKGROUND', (0, 0), (-1, 0), colors.grey),
    ('TEXTCOLOR', (0, 0), (-1, 0), colors.whitesmoke),
    ('ALIGN', (0, 0), (-1, -1), 'CENTER'),
    ('FONTNAME', (0, 0), (-1, 0), 'Helvetica-Bold'),
    ('FONTSIZE', (0, 0), (-1, 0), 12),
    ('BOTTOMPADDING', (0, 0), (-1, 0), 12),
    ('BACKGROUND', (0, 1), (-1, -1), colors.beige),
    ('GRID', (0, 0), (-1, -1), 1, colors.black)
]))
story.append(table)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Section 2: Regional Performance
story.append(Paragraph("Regional Performance", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph(
    "North America led growth with 20% increase, followed by Europe at 15%...",
    styles['Normal']
))
story.append(Spacer(1, 0.3*inch))

# Section 3: Future Outlook
story.append(Paragraph("Future Outlook", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph(
    "Looking ahead to Q1 2025, we anticipate continued momentum with...",
    styles['Normal']
))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
print("Created Q4_2024_Sales_Report.pdf")

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
• Professional multi-page PDF report
  • Formatted title, sections, and body text
  • Table with styling and borders
  • Page breaks between major sections

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: Combine multiple invoice PDFs into a single document for archiving.

docs.title: Conversation
docs.text:
User: Merge all PDF files in the invoices/ directory into a single archive file

Claude: I'll use pypdf to merge all PDFs while preserving their content.

from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader
from pathlib import Path

writer = PdfWriter()
invoices_dir = Path("invoices")
pdf_files = sorted(invoices_dir.glob("*.pdf"))

if not pdf_files:
    print("No PDF files found in invoices/ directory")
else:
    for pdf_file in pdf_files:
        print(f"Adding {pdf_file.name}...")
        reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
        for page in reader.pages:
            writer.add_page(page)

    # Add metadata
    writer.add_metadata({
        '/Title': 'Invoice Archive',

docs.text:
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path

pdf_files = Path("documents").glob("*.pdf")
results = []

for pdf_file in pdf_files:
    try:
        reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
        results.append({
            'file': pdf_file.name,
            'pages': len(reader.pages),
            'status': 'success'
        })
    except Exception as e:
        results.append({
            'file': pdf_file.name,
            'pages': 0,
            'status': f'error: {str(e)}'
        })

# Summary

for result in results:
    print(f"  {result['file']}: {result['pages']} pages - {result['status']}")

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Philosopher Analyst skill enables Claude to perform deep conceptual analysis and argument evaluation. Drawing on logic, epistemology, metaphysics, and philosophical traditions, this skill provides insights into meaning, truth, knowledge, existence, and reasoning.

docs.title: What Makes This Different
docs.text:
Unlike general critical thinking, philosopher analysis:

  1. Conceptual Precision: Defines terms rigorously, exposing ambiguities
  2. Logical Rigor: Evaluates validity and soundness systematically
  3. Assumption Excavation: Makes hidden premises explicit
  4. Multiple Traditions: Integrates analytic, continental, and Eastern perspectives
  5. Argument Charity: Interprets positions in strongest form
  6. Deep Questions: Addresses fundamental issues about knowledge, reality, meaning

docs.text:
• Conceptual Analysis: Clarify vague concepts, resolve ambiguities
  • Argument Evaluation: Assess logical validity, identify fallacies
  • Epistemology: What can we know? How do we know it?
  • Metaphysics: Nature of reality, identity, causation, time
  • Philosophy of Science: Scientific methods, theory change, realism
  • Philosophy of Mind: Consciousness, free will, mental causation
  • Logic: Formal and informal reasoning, symbolic logic

docs.text:

docs.title: Analysis Process
docs.text:
1. Clarify Question - Disambiguate, distinguish empirical from conceptual
  2. Define Terms - Precise definitions, consistent usage
  3. Identify Assumptions - Make implicit premises explicit
  4. Reconstruct Arguments - Premises, conclusions, hidden steps
  5. Evaluate Validity - Do conclusions follow logically?
  6. Evaluate Soundness - Are premises true?
  7. Consider Objections - Strongest counterarguments
  8. Apply Frameworks - Multiple philosophical perspectives
  9. Explore Implications - Logical consequences
  10. Reflective Equilibrium - Coherent position with appropriate confidence

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Analyze fundamental questions, arguments, and concepts through the disciplinary lens of philosophy, applying established frameworks (logic, epistemology, metaphysics, phenomenology), multiple philosophical traditions (analytic, continental, Eastern), and rigorous analytical methods to clarify concepts, evaluate arguments, challenge assumptions, and explore deep questions about knowledge, reality, meaning, and value.

docs.title: When to Use This Skill
docs.text:

  • Argument Evaluation: Assess logical validity, soundness, and fallacies in reasoning
  • Epistemological Questions: Examine what we can know and how we know it
  • Metaphysical Questions: Explore nature of reality, existence, causation, time, identity
  • Philosophy of Science: Analyze scientific methods, theories, and presuppositions
  • Philosophy of Mind: Consciousness, mental states, mind-body problem, free will
  • Political Philosophy: Justice, authority, liberty, rights, social contract

docs.title: Core Philosophy: Philosophical Thinking
docs.text:
Philosophical analysis rests on several fundamental principles:

Conceptual Clarity: Philosophy begins with clear definitions. Vague concepts breed confused thinking. Precision in language is essential to intellectual progress.

Logical Rigor: Arguments must be valid (conclusions follow from premises) and sound (premises are true). Informal fallacies and logical errors undermine reasoning.

Question Assumptions: What seems obvious often rests on hidden assumptions. Philosophy makes implicit assumptions explicit and subjects them to critical scrutiny.

Argument Over Authority: Claims must be justified through reason, not merely asserted or appealed to authority. Everyone's arguments stand on equal footing before reason.

Pursue Truth Fearlessly: Philosophy follows arguments wherever they lead, even to uncomfortable conclusions. Intellectual honesty requires accepting logical consequences.

Acknowledge Limitations: Many questions have no certain answers. Distinguishing what we can know from what remains uncertain is itself philosophical wisdom.

Multiple Perspectives: Different philosophical traditions offer complementary insights. Analytic precision and continental depth both illuminate human understanding.

Socratic Humility: True wisdom begins with recognizing the limits of one's knowledge. The unexamined life, and the unexamined argument, is not worth holding.

docs.title: Foundation 1: Logic and Argumentation
docs.text:
Core Principles:

  • Validity: Argument is valid if conclusion necessarily follows from premises
  • Soundness: Argument is sound if valid AND premises are true
  • Deductive reasoning: Necessarily truth-preserving (if premises true, conclusion must be true)
  • Inductive reasoning: Probabilistically truth-preserving (premises support conclusion)
  • Formal logic: Symbolic representation of arguments (propositional, predicate, modal logic)
  • Informal logic: Argument analysis in natural language, fallacy identification

Key Insights:

  • Valid argument can have false conclusion if premises false
  • Invalid argument can have true conclusion (by accident)
  • Soundness requires both validity and true premises
  • Most real-world reasoning is inductive or abductive, not purely deductive
  • Informal fallacies are persuasive but logically flawed patterns
  • Conditional reasoning (if-then) frequently misused (affirming consequent, denying antecedent)

Common Fallacies:

  • Ad hominem: Attack person, not argument
  • Straw man: Misrepresent opponent's position
  • Appeal to authority: Expert opinion as proof
  • False dichotomy: Present only two options when more exist
  • Begging the question: Assume what trying to prove
  • Post hoc ergo propter hoc: Correlation implies causation
  • Slippery slope: Claim without showing causal chain
  • Equivocation: Use word with shifting meaning

Founding Thinkers:

  • Aristotle (384-322 BCE): Formal logic, syllogisms, Organon
  • Gottlob Frege (1848-1925): Modern symbolic logic, predicate calculus
  • Bertrand Russell (1872-1970): Principia Mathematica, logical atomism

When to Apply:

  • Evaluating arguments for validity and soundness
  • Identifying logical fallacies
  • Constructing rigorous proofs
  • Analyzing policy debates and reasoning
  • Teaching critical thinking

Sources:

  • Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Logic
  • Stanford Encyclopedia: Logic
  • Formal Logic - Bergmann et al.

docs.title: Foundation 2: Epistemology (Theory of Knowledge)
docs.text:
Core Principles:

  • Justified True Belief (JTB): Traditional analysis of knowledge
  • Gettier Problems: Show JTB insufficient for knowledge
  • Foundationalism: Knowledge rests on basic, self-evident beliefs
  • Coherentism: Beliefs justified by coherence with belief system
  • Reliabilism: Belief counts as knowledge if produced by reliable process
  • Skepticism: Doubt possibility of knowledge, especially about external world

Key Insights:

  • Knowledge requires more than true belief; justification matters
  • Justification standards vary: infallibilism (certainty) vs. fallibilism (reasonable confidence)
  • Testimony and trust are essential to knowledge; we can't verify everything ourselves
  • A priori knowledge (known independently of experience) vs. a posteriori (empirical)
  • Rationalism (reason primary) vs. empiricism (experience primary)
  • Social epistemology: Knowledge is collective, not just individual

Classical Problems:

  • Problem of Induction: Why believe future will resemble past? (Hume)
  • Problem of Other Minds: How know others have minds?
  • External World Skepticism: Can we know material world exists? (Descartes' demon)
  • Gettier Cases: True justified belief that isn't knowledge

Founding Thinkers:

  • Plato (428-348 BCE): Theaetetus, knowledge as justified true belief
  • René Descartes (1596-1650): Meditations, methodical doubt, cogito ergo sum
  • David Hume (1711-1776): Empiricism, problem of induction, skepticism
  • Immanuel Kant (1724-1804): Synthetic a priori, transcendental idealism
  • Edmund Gettier (1927-2021): Gettier problems challenged JTB account

When to Apply:

  • Assessing knowledge claims and justification
  • Understanding limits of knowledge
  • Evaluating scientific methods and inference
  • Analyzing testimony and expertise
  • Exploring certainty vs. reasonable belief

Sources:

  • Epistemology - Stanford Encyclopedia
  • Knowledge Analysis - IEP
  • Theory of Knowledge - Audi

docs.title: Foundation 3: Metaphysics (Nature of Reality)
docs.text:
Core Principles:

  • Ontology: What exists? Categories of being
  • Identity: What makes something the same over time? (persistence, personal identity)
  • Causation: What is causal connection? Laws of nature?
  • Time: Is time real or illusion? Presentism vs. eternalism
  • Modality: Necessity, possibility, contingency; possible worlds
  • Universals vs. Particulars: Do properties exist independently of instances?

Key Insights:

  • Ship of Theseus: If all parts replaced, is it same ship?
  • Sorites paradox: Vague predicates create borderline cases (heap of sand)
  • Mind-body problem: How mental states relate to physical states
  • Free will vs. determinism: Can choices be free if causally determined?
  • Composition: When do parts constitute a whole?
  • Mereology: Study of parts and wholes

Major Positions:

  • Materialism/Physicalism: Only physical things exist
  • Idealism: Reality fundamentally mental (Berkeley)
  • Dualism: Mental and physical both fundamental (Descartes)
  • Neutral monism: Mental and physical are aspects of neutral substance

Founding Thinkers:

  • Aristotle (384-322 BCE): Metaphysics, substance, causation, potentiality/actuality
  • David Hume (1711-1776): Skepticism about causation, personal identity
  • Immanuel Kant (1724-1804): Phenomena vs. noumena, conditions of experience
  • Saul Kripke (1940-present): Naming and Necessity, rigid designators, necessity

When to Apply:

  • Conceptual puzzles about identity, change, persistence
  • Philosophy of science (causation, laws, explanation)
  • Mind-body problem and consciousness
  • Free will debates
  • Clarifying what exists and what categories

Sources:

  • Metaphysics - Stanford Encyclopedia
  • Metaphysics - Loux

docs.title: Foundation 4: Philosophy of Science
docs.text:
Core Principles:

  • Scientific Method: Observation, hypothesis, prediction, testing, revision
  • Demarcation Problem: What distinguishes science from non-science?
  • Theory and Observation: Observations theory-laden; no pure observation
  • Underdetermination: Multiple theories compatible with same evidence
  • Scientific Realism: Successful theories approximately true, entities real
  • Instrumentalism: Theories are tools for prediction, not literal truth

Key Insights:

  • Science doesn't prove, it corroborates or falsifies (Popper)
  • Paradigm shifts restructure scientific worldview (Kuhn)
  • No algorithm for discovery; creativity essential
  • Scientific consensus emerges from critical community, not authority
  • Models and idealizations essential but literally false
  • Social factors influence science but don't determine it

Major Debates:

  • Realism vs. Anti-realism: Do unobservables (electrons, genes) really exist?
  • Theory Change: Progress or paradigm shifts? (Kuhn vs. Lakatos)
  • Explanation: Deductive-nomological vs. causal-mechanical vs. unification
  • Reduction: Can higher-level sciences reduce to physics?

Founding Thinkers:

  • Karl Popper (1902-1994): Falsificationism, demarcation, Logic of Scientific Discovery
  • Thomas Kuhn (1922-1996): Structure of Scientific Revolutions, paradigms, incommensurability
  • Imre Lakatos (1922-1974): Research programmes, sophisticated falsificationism
  • Bas van Fraassen (1941-present): Constructive empiricism

When to Apply:

  • Evaluating scientific claims and methods
  • Understanding theory choice and evidence
  • Assessing pseudoscience claims
  • Philosophy of specific sciences (physics, biology, social sciences)
  • Scientific realism debates

Sources:

  • Philosophy of Science - Stanford Encyclopedia
  • Kuhn: Structure of Scientific Revolutions
  • Popper: Logic of Scientific Discovery

docs.title: Foundation 5: Philosophy of Mind and Consciousness
docs.text:
Core Principles:

  • Mind-Body Problem: How do mental states relate to physical brain states?
  • Qualia: Subjective, qualitative character of experience ("what it's like")
  • Intentionality: Aboutness of mental states (beliefs are about something)
  • Consciousness: Phenomenal (subjective experience) vs. access (information availability)
  • Free Will: Can choices be free if universe is deterministic?

Key Insights:

  • Hard problem of consciousness: Why is there subjective experience at all?
  • Explanatory gap: Physical facts don't logically entail facts about consciousness
  • Zombie thought experiment: Physically identical being without consciousness
  • Chinese Room: Computation alone insufficient for understanding (Searle)
  • Multiple realizability: Mental states can be realized in different physical substrates
  • Emergentism: Consciousness emerges from but isn't reducible to physical processes

Major Positions:

  • Dualism: Mind and body distinct substances (Descartes)
  • Physicalism/Materialism: Mental states are physical states
  • Identity theory: Mental states identical to brain states
  • Functionalism: Mental states defined by causal roles
  • Eliminativism: Folk psychology false; mental states don't exist
  • Property Dualism: One substance, two types of properties
  • Panpsychism: Consciousness fundamental feature of universe

Founding Thinkers:

  • René Descartes (1596-1650): Mind-body dualism, cogito
  • Gilbert Ryle (1900-1976): Attacked Cartesian "ghost in machine"
  • Thomas Nagel (1937-present): "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", subjective character
  • John Searle (1932-present): Chinese Room argument, biological naturalism
  • David Chalmers (1966-present): Hard problem of consciousness

When to Apply:

  • Consciousness research and AI
  • Personal identity and persistence
  • Free will and moral responsibility
  • Animal consciousness and ethics
  • Mental causation problems

Sources:

  • Philosophy of Mind - Stanford Encyclopedia
  • Consciousness - IEP
  • Chalmers: The Conscious Mind

docs.title: Framework 1: Socratic Method (Dialectical Questioning)
docs.text:
Overview: Expose contradictions and clarify concepts through systematic questioning.

Process:

  1. Claim: Begin with a claim or definition
  2. Clarification: Ask for explanation and examples
  3. Probing assumptions: What assumptions underlie this?
  4. Evidence/reasoning: What supports this claim?
  5. Alternative perspectives: What would someone who disagrees say?
  6. Implications: What follows if this is true?
  7. Question the question: Is this the right question to ask?

Goals:

  • Expose hidden contradictions
  • Clarify vague concepts
  • Reveal assumptions
  • Stimulate critical thinking
  • Intellectual humility

When to Use: Teaching, exploring unclear concepts, challenging dogma, philosophical inquiry

Sources: Socratic Method - Stanford Encyclopedia

docs.title: Framework 2: Conceptual Analysis
docs.text:
Overview: Analyze concepts by seeking necessary and sufficient conditions.

Process:

  1. Initial definition: Propose necessary and sufficient conditions
  2. Test with examples: Does definition capture all instances?
  3. Counterexamples: Find cases that violate definition
  4. Refine: Adjust definition to handle counterexamples
  5. Iterate: Repeat until reflective equilibrium

Example - Knowledge:

  • Initial: Knowledge = justified true belief
  • Gettier counterexample: JTB without knowledge
  • Refinement: Add "no essential false lemmas" or other conditions
  • Further refinement: Reliabilism, virtue epistemology, etc.

When to Use: Clarifying concepts, resolving ambiguity, philosophical analysis

docs.title: Framework 3: Thought Experiments
docs.text:
Overview: Explore concepts and intuitions through hypothetical scenarios.

Famous Examples:

  • Brain in a Vat (Epistemology): Could you be a brain stimulated to have false experiences?
  • Chinese Room (Philosophy of Mind): Can computation alone produce understanding?
  • Ship of Theseus (Metaphysics): If all parts replaced, is it the same ship?
  • Trolley Problem (Ethics): When permissible to sacrifice one to save five?
  • Veil of Ignorance (Political Philosophy): What's just if you don't know your position?
  • Mary's Room (Consciousness): Does neuroscientist who sees color for first time learn something new?
  • Philosophical Zombie (Consciousness): Is physical duplicate without consciousness conceivable?

Purpose:

  • Isolate variables and clarify intuitions
  • Test principles against edge cases
  • Reveal commitments and conceptual connections
  • Challenge received views

When to Use: Testing philosophical theories, eliciting intuitions, teaching philosophy

Sources: Thought Experiments - Stanford Encyclopedia

docs.title: Framework 4: Argument Mapping
docs.text:
Overview: Visual representation of argument structure.

Components:

  • Premises: Supporting statements (numbered)
  • Intermediate conclusions: Follow from subset of premises
  • Main conclusion: Ultimate claim being defended
  • Objections: Counterarguments to premises or inferences
  • Rebuttals: Responses to objections

Benefits:

  • Makes argument structure explicit
  • Reveals hidden premises
  • Identifies weak links
  • Facilitates evaluation
  • Enhances clarity in complex debates

When to Use: Complex arguments, philosophical papers, policy debates, teaching

Tools: Rationale, Argunet, MindMup

docs.title: Framework 5: Principle of Charity
docs.text:
Overview: Interpret arguments in strongest, most reasonable form.

Guidelines:

  1. Assume rationality: Interpret to avoid obvious errors
  2. Fill in gaps: Supply missing premises if reasonable
  3. Disambiguate: Choose most charitable interpretation of ambiguous claims
  4. Focus on strongest version: Address best form of opponent's argument
  5. Avoid straw-manning: Don't misrepresent to make refutation easier

Rationale:

  • Productive dialogue requires understanding opponent's actual view
  • Defeating weak version doesn't show position flawed
  • Charity facilitates learning from disagreement
  • Intellectual honesty demands fairness

When to Use: Argument evaluation, philosophical dialogue, teaching, debates

docs.title: Methodology 1: Analytic Philosophy Approach
docs.text:
Description: Emphasis on logical rigor, conceptual clarity, and argument analysis.

Characteristics:

  • Logical analysis of language and concepts
  • Formal methods when applicable (logic, probability)
  • Piecemeal problem-solving rather than system-building
  • Engagement with science and mathematics
  • Clarity and precision in expression

Representative Figures: Russell, Wittgenstein, Quine, Kripke, Lewis

When to Apply: Conceptual analysis, logic problems, philosophy of science, epistemology

docs.title: Methodology 2: Continental Philosophy Approach
docs.text:
Description: Focus on human experience, existence, interpretation, and historical context.

Characteristics:

  • Phenomenology: Study of structures of experience
  • Hermeneutics: Theory of interpretation
  • Historical consciousness and tradition
  • Existential and ethical concerns foregrounded
  • Literary and interpretive styles

Representative Figures: Heidegger, Sartre, Merleau-Ponty, Gadamer, Foucault, Derrida

When to Apply: Questions of meaning, existence, interpretation, human condition, social critique

docs.title: Methodology 3: Pragmatism
docs.text:
Description: Evaluate beliefs and concepts by practical consequences and utility.

Core Ideas:

  • Truth is what works
  • Meaning is tied to practical consequences
  • Inquiry is continuous process, not search for certainty
  • Anti-foundationalism: No fixed foundations of knowledge
  • Fallibilism: All beliefs revisable in light of experience

Representative Figures: Peirce, James, Dewey, Quine, Rorty

When to Apply: Evaluating theories instrumentally, practical reasoning, rejecting dogmatism

docs.title: Methodology 4: Eastern Philosophical Traditions
docs.text:
Description: Non-Western approaches emphasizing practice, non-dualism, liberation.

Traditions:

  • Buddhism: No-self (anātman), emptiness (śūnyatā), dependent origination, suffering and its cessation
  • Taoism: Dao (Way), wu wei (effortless action), naturalism, complementary opposites
  • Confucianism: Virtue cultivation, social harmony, ritual propriety (li), humaneness (ren)
  • Vedanta: Brahman (ultimate reality), Atman (self), non-dualism, liberation (moksha)

Key Differences from Western Philosophy:

  • Practice-oriented (meditation, cultivation)
  • Holistic and non-dualistic thinking
  • Less emphasis on logical argument, more on experience and wisdom
  • Integration of philosophy and spirituality

When to Apply: Comparative philosophy, consciousness studies, ethics, meaning questions

docs.title: Methodology 5: Phenomenology
docs.text:
Description: Study phenomena as they appear to consciousness.

Process:

  1. Epoché (bracketing): Suspend judgments about external reality
  2. Phenomenological reduction: Focus on structures of experience itself
  3. Eidetic variation: Imaginatively vary features to identify essences
  4. Intentionality analysis: Examine directedness of consciousness toward objects
  5. Lifeworld description: Describe pre-theoretical lived experience

Applications: Consciousness, perception, embodiment, intersubjectivity

Founding Thinker: Edmund Husserl (1859-1938)

docs.title: Example 1: Gettier Problem and Analysis of Knowledge
docs.text:
Problem: Is justified true belief sufficient for knowledge?

Philosophical Analysis:

Classical Definition (Plato): S knows that p if and only if:

  1. p is true
  2. S believes that p
  3. S is justified in believing that p

Gettier Counterexample (1963): Smith and Jones have applied for the same job. Smith has strong evidence for: (e) Jones will get the job, and Jones has 10 coins in his pocket

From (e), Smith infers: (f) The man who will get the job has 10 coins in his pocket

Smith's reasoning seems justified. Suppose:

  • (f) is true
  • Smith believes (f)
  • Smith is justified in believing (f)

But: Smith actually gets the job, and Smith has 10 coins in his pocket (coincidentally).

Analysis:

  • Smith has justified true belief that (f)
  • But intuitively, Smith doesn't know (f)
  • Justification based on false belief (e)
  • Conclusion: JTB is insufficient for knowledge

Philosophical Responses:

1. No False Lemmas Condition:

  • Add: Justification must not essentially rely on false beliefs
  • Problem: Artificial? What counts as "essential"?

2. Reliabilism:

  • Knowledge = true belief formed by reliable process
  • Smith's belief not from reliable process (true by luck)
  • Problem: Undermines role of justification?

3. Virtue Epistemology:

  • Knowledge = true belief from intellectual virtues
  • Smith's belief not from virtue (lucky guess based on false assumption)

4. Safety Condition:

  • Belief must be safe: couldn't easily have been false in nearby possible worlds
  • Smith's belief not safe (Jones nearly got job)

5. Sensitivity Condition:

  • If p were false, S wouldn't believe p
  • Smith's belief not sensitive (would still believe based on false e)

Key Insight: Gettier cases show knowledge requires more than JTB. Exact requirement remains debated 60+ years later. Illustrates how single counterexample can overturn centuries-old philosophical consensus.

Sources:

  • Gettier: Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?
  • Analysis of Knowledge - Stanford Encyclopedia

docs.title: Example 2: Chinese Room Argument and Strong AI
docs.text:
Question: Can computers understand language or just manipulate symbols?

Philosophical Analysis:

Searle's Thought Experiment (1980):

  • Imagine person in room with Chinese symbols
  • Person has rulebook (in English) for manipulating symbols
  • Chinese speakers outside pass questions (symbols) into room
  • Person follows rules to produce output symbols (answers)
  • To Chinese speakers, room appears to understand Chinese
  • But person inside doesn't understand Chinese, just follows rules

Argument:

  1. Person in room doesn't understand Chinese (just follows syntax rules)
  2. Person implements computer program
  3. Therefore, implementing program doesn't produce understanding
  4. Strong AI claims digital computers can literally understand
  5. Therefore, Strong AI is false

Replies and Counter-Replies:

Systems Reply:

  • Individual doesn't understand, but system (person + rulebook + room) does
  • Searle: Internalize rules; person still doesn't understand

Robot Reply:

  • Add sensory input and motor output (embodied cognition)
  • Searle: Add perceptual rules; still just symbol manipulation

Brain Simulator Reply:

  • Simulate brain's causal structure at neuron level
  • Searle: Still formal manipulation; intrinsic intentionality missing

Other Minds Reply:

  • Same skepticism applies to other humans
  • We infer understanding from behavior
  • Searle: Humans have right causal powers (biological); computers don't

Connectionists:

  • Brain doesn't follow rules like symbolic AI
  • Neural networks are different
  • Searle: Still formal operations; substrate irrelevant to argument

Philosophical Issues:

Syntax vs. Semantics:

  • Computation is syntactic (form-based)
  • Understanding requires semantics (meaning)
  • Syntax alone insufficient for semantics

Intentionality:

  • Mental states have intentionality (aboutness)
  • Derived intentionality (words, computers) vs. intrinsic (minds)
  • Can derived intentionality become intrinsic?

Functionalism Challenge:

  • Functionalism: Mental states defined by causal roles
  • Chinese Room challenges: Same functional organization, no understanding
  • Blocks functionalism as sufficient for mentality

Implications:

  • For AI: Computation alone may be insufficient for genuine intelligence
  • For Cognitive Science: Challenges computational theory of mind
  • For Consciousness: Suggests consciousness requires more than information processing
  • For Philosophy of Mind: Functionalism may be inadequate

Counter-Perspective:

  • Searle's intuition may be wrong
  • Understanding is gradual, not all-or-nothing
  • System as whole may understand even if components don't
  • Biological chauvinism: Why must understanding be biological?

Key Insight: Chinese Room argument challenges the computational theory of mind by arguing that syntax (form) is insufficient for semantics (meaning). Whether Searle's intuition is correct remains deeply contested, but argument has profoundly influenced philosophy of mind and AI.

Sources:

  • Searle: Minds, Brains, and Programs
  • Chinese Room Argument - Stanford Encyclopedia

docs.title: Example 3: Personal Identity and the Ship of Theseus
docs.text:
Question: What makes a person the same person over time despite physical and psychological changes?

Philosophical Analysis:

Ship of Theseus Paradox:

  • Theseus's ship gradually has all planks replaced
  • After complete replacement, is it the same ship?
  • Suppose original planks reassembled into ship
  • Which ship is Theseus's ship?

Application to Personal Identity:

  • Bodies' atoms completely replaced over 7-10 years
  • Memories, beliefs, personality change
  • What makes you the same person you were 20 years ago?

Competing Theories:

1. Bodily Continuity Theory:

  • You are same person if same living body
  • Problems: Gradual replacement of cells; brain transplant cases
  • Modified: Continuity of brain (or specific brain regions)

2. Psychological Continuity Theory (Locke):

  • You are same person if psychological continuity (memories, personality, beliefs)
  • Chain of overlapping memories and character traits
  • Problems: Memory loss (Alzheimer's), split brain cases

3. Narrative Self Theory:

  • Personal identity constructed through life narrative
  • You are the story you tell about yourself
  • Problems: False memories, revisionist histories

4. No-Self Theory (Buddhist, Hume):

  • No enduring self; just bundle of perceptions
  • Personal identity is convenient fiction
  • Problems: Practical necessity of identity; first-person perspective

Thought Experiments:

Brain Transplant:

  • Your brain transplanted into another body
  • Where are "you"? In original body (now vegetative) or new body with your brain?
  • Most: You go with brain (psychological continuity)

Split Brain:

  • Brain divided, each half transplanted into body
  • Two people now have your psychology
  • Which is you? Both? Neither?
  • Challenges psychological criterion (branching problem)

Teletransportation (Parfit):

  • Device scans your body, destroys it, recreates exact copy on Mars
  • Is person on Mars you, or just a replica?
  • Continuity or identity?

Fission Case:

  • You divide into two people with your psychology
  • Psychological continuity without identity (can't be identical to two distinct people)
  • Conclusion: Continuity matters more than identity

Parfit's View:

  • Personal identity not what matters
  • Psychological continuity and connectedness matter
  • Survival admits degrees
  • Identity doesn't

Implications:

  • Ethics: If no enduring self, how understand moral responsibility?
  • Prudential: Should I care about my future self? (If psychological continuity weak)
  • Death: Is death extinction or transformation?
  • Cryonics: If revived centuries later, would be "you"?
  • Mind Uploading: Would digital copy be you or copy?

Key Insight: Personal identity puzzles reveal that our commonsense notion of self may not map onto clear metaphysical fact. We may need to reconceptualize identity, or accept that questions like "Is this the same person?" lack determinate answers in all cases.

Sources:

  • Personal Identity - Stanford Encyclopedia
  • Parfit: Reasons and Persons

docs.title: Analysis Process
docs.text: When using the philosopher-analyst skill, follow this systematic 10-step process:

docs.title: Step 1: Clarify the Question
docs.text:
• What exactly is being asked?
  • Is this empirical question or conceptual/normative?
  • What ambiguities need resolving?

docs.title: Step 2: Define Key Terms
docs.text:
• What do central concepts mean?
  • Are terms being used consistently?
  • Do definitions beg the question?

docs.title: Step 3: Identify Assumptions
docs.text:
• What is being taken for granted?
  • Are assumptions justified?
  • What happens if assumptions rejected?

docs.title: Step 4: Reconstruct Arguments
docs.text:
• What are premises and conclusions?
  • Are there hidden premises?
  • Is argument deductive or inductive?

docs.title: Step 5: Evaluate Validity
docs.text:
• Do conclusions follow from premises?
  • Identify logical form
  • Check for formal fallacies

docs.title: Step 6: Evaluate Soundness
docs.text:
• Are premises true?
  • What evidence supports them?
  • Are there counterexamples?

docs.title: Step 7: Consider Objections
docs.text:
• What would critics say?
  • Strongest counterarguments?
  • Are objections decisive?

docs.title: Step 8: Apply Philosophical Frameworks
docs.text:
• What do different traditions say?
  • Analytic, continental, Eastern perspectives?
  • Historical context?

docs.title: Step 9: Explore Implications
docs.text:
• What follows if position accepted?
  • Consistency with other beliefs?
  • Practical consequences?

docs.title: Step 10: Reach Reflective Equilibrium
docs.text:
• Adjust beliefs and principles for coherence
  • Acknowledge uncertainties
  • State position with appropriate confidence

docs.title: Quality Standards
docs.text:
A thorough philosophical analysis includes:

✓ Conceptual clarity: Key terms precisely defined ✓ Logical rigor: Arguments valid, fallacies identified ✓ Explicit assumptions: Hidden premises made visible ✓ Charitable interpretation: Strongest form of positions considered ✓ Multiple perspectives: Different philosophical traditions engaged ✓ Counterarguments addressed: Objections taken seriously ✓ Implications explored: Logical consequences traced ✓ Appropriate modesty: Limits of knowledge acknowledged ✓ Clear communication: Accessible to non-specialists where possible ✓ Intellectual honesty: Following arguments where they lead

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This quiz validates that the philosopher analyst applies philosophical methods correctly, identifies conceptual distinctions and logical structures, and provides well-grounded philosophical analysis. Each scenario requires demonstration of philosophical reasoning, critical thinking, and systematic argumentation.

docs.title: Scenario 1: The Ship of Theseus and Personal Identity
docs.text:
Event Description: A person undergoes gradual brain augmentation over 20 years. Initially, a small neural implant assists memory formation (5% of brain function). Over time, more implants replace damaged neural tissue following strokes and degenerative disease. By year 20, 60% of cognitive functions run on synthetic neural processors, seamlessly integrated with remaining biological neurons. The person's memories, personality, and consciousness remain continuous throughout - they feel like "the same person" at each step. However, philosophers debate: Is this still the original person? If biological substrate matters for identity, at what threshold (10%? 50%? 90% replacement) did the original person cease to exist and a new entity begin? If psychological continuity matters, then identity persists regardless of substrate. The case is complicated when, at year 25, the biological brain fails completely and the person's mind runs entirely on synthetic neural networks. Family members must decide whether to maintain the digital consciousness or allow it to end.

Analysis Task: Analyze the philosophical problems of personal identity and persistence over time.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• The Ship of Theseus Problem:
  • Classical formulation: If all parts of a ship are gradually replaced, is it the same ship?
  • Puzzle of persistence: What makes an entity the same entity over time despite change?
  • Gradual vs. sudden replacement: Does rate of change matter?
  • Application: Brain augmentation as biological Theseus ship

  • Paradox: Continuity of experience vs. continuity of substrate

  • Theories of Personal Identity:

  • Psychological continuity theory (Locke, Parfit): Identity based on memories, beliefs, personality
    • Supports: Person feels continuous, memories/personality intact
    • Problems: Memory can be transferred to new substrate (is that the same person?)
  • Biological/physical continuity (animalism): Identity tied to living organism
    • Supports: Bodily continuity matters (brain is biological organ)
    • Problems: Gradual replacement undermines clear biological continuity
  • Narrative identity (Ricoeur, MacIntyre): Self as coherent life story
    • Supports: Person's narrative is continuous
    • Problems: Narrative can be preserved in any substrate (even AI)

  • No-self view (Buddhist, Hume, Parfit): No enduring self, only bundles of experiences

    • Supports: Avoids reification of "self," accepts change
    • Problems: Conflicts with intuition of persistent identity

  • Thought Experiments and Intuition Pumps:

  • Teleportation case (Parfit): If body is destroyed and replica created, is it same person?
  • Brain bisection: If brain split and each half transferred to new body, which is original person?
  • Gradual neuron replacement: Chinese Nation thought experiment (Searle) - functional equivalence
  • Swampman (Davidson): Molecule-for-molecule duplicate created by lightning - is it same person?

  • Fission and fusion cases: What if one person splits into two?

  • Sorites Paradox (Heap Paradox):

  • Classical: Removing one grain from heap doesn't stop it being heap, but eventually it's not a heap
  • Application: Replacing 1% of brain doesn't change identity, but at some point identity changes
  • Vague predicates: "Same person" may lack sharp boundaries
  • Solutions: Accept vagueness (epistemicism, supervaluationism) or deny sharp identity

  • Tolerance principle: Small changes can't affect identity (but accumulate to large change)

  • Substrate Independence vs. Dependence:

  • Functionalism: Mental states are functional states (multiple realizability - can run on different substrates)
  • Biological essentialism: Mind requires biological substrate (carbon chauvinism objection)
  • Consciousness and qualia: Can synthetic neurons support phenomenal experience?
  • Uploading: If mind is pattern of information, can it be instantiated in computer?

  • Intuitions diverge: Many accept gradual replacement but reject sudden uploading

  • Moral and Practical Implications:

  • Moral status: If identity persists, synthetic person has same moral rights as biological
  • End-of-life decisions: Is "pulling the plug" on digital mind murder? Euthanasia?
  • Legal personhood: Should digital consciousness have legal rights? Inheritance?
  • Family relationships: Are obligations to biological person transferred to synthetic successor?

  • Precautionary approach: Uncertainty about identity suggests caution

  • Metaphysical Questions:

  • Persistence conditions: What are necessary and sufficient conditions for identity over time?
  • Diachronic vs. synchronic identity: Same person at different times vs. same person at one time
  • Endurantism vs. perdurantism: Object wholly present at each moment vs. temporal parts
  • Four-dimensionalism: Person as spacetime worm extending through time

  • Conventionalism: "Same person" is conventional, not metaphysical fact

  • Historical and Philosophical Context:

  • Theseus' Ship: Plutarch (1st century CE), earliest formulation
  • John Locke: "Essay Concerning Human Understanding" (1689) - memory theory of personal identity
  • David Hume: "Treatise on Human Nature" (1739) - bundle theory, no enduring self
  • Derek Parfit: "Reasons and Persons" (1984) - psychological continuity, reductionism about identity
  • Bernard Williams: "The Self and the Future" (1970) - bodily continuity matters
  • Sydney Shoemaker & Richard Swinburne: "Personal Identity" (1984) - debate
  • Buddhist philosophy: Anatman (no-self) doctrine

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct application of philosophical concepts, theories, distinctions
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of conceptual analysis, argument evaluation, implications
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear philosophical reasoning, specific theory application
  • Historical Grounding (0-10): References to philosophical traditions, thought experiments
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical coherence, structured argumentation

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scenario 2: The Trolley Problem and Doctrine of Double Effect
docs.text:
Event Description: A runaway trolley speeds toward five railway workers who will certainly die if struck. You stand next to a lever that can divert the trolley onto a side track, where it will kill one worker instead. Three related scenarios: (A) You can pull the lever, diverting the trolley to kill one instead of five. (B) You stand on a footbridge above the tracks with a large stranger; pushing them onto the tracks will stop the trolley, saving five but killing the pushed person. (C) You are a doctor with five dying patients needing organs; you could kill one healthy patient and distribute their organs, saving five. Surveys show 90% endorse pulling lever (A), but only 10% endorse pushing (B), and 5% endorse killing for organs (C). Yet all three cases involve killing one to save five - why do moral intuitions diverge?

Analysis Task: Analyze the trolley problem and the moral principles underlying divergent intuitions.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Consequentialist vs. Deontological Frameworks:
  • Consequentialism (utilitarianism): Rightness determined by outcomes (maximize welfare, minimize deaths)
    • Supports lever-pulling, pushing, organ harvesting (all save net 4 lives)
    • Impartial calculation: 5 lives > 1 life
  • Deontology (Kantian): Rightness determined by duties, rules, respect for persons
    • Opposes using person as mere means (pushing, organ harvesting violate Kant's Formula of Humanity)
    • Prohibitions against killing (even to save others) take priority

  • Tension: Utilitarian and deontological principles conflict in these cases

  • Doctrine of Double Effect (DDE):

  • Principle: Permissible to cause foreseeable harm as side effect of pursuing good, but not as means
  • Four conditions: (1) Act itself not intrinsically wrong, (2) Good effect intended, bad effect foreseen but not intended, (3) Bad effect not means to good effect, (4) Proportionality (good outweighs bad)
  • Lever case: Death of one is side effect (not means) of diverting trolley (satisfies DDE)
  • Push case: Death of one is means to stopping trolley (violates DDE)
  • Organ case: Killing patient is means to obtaining organs (violates DDE)

  • DDE explains divergent intuitions: Lever pulling permissible, pushing/organ harvesting impermissible

  • Killing vs. Letting Die Distinction:

  • Active killing: Directly causing death (pushing, organ harvesting)
  • Passive allowing: Failing to prevent death (not pulling lever = letting five die)
  • Lever case complication: Pulling lever is active intervention, but kills one rather than letting five die
  • Moral relevance: Is there intrinsic moral difference between killing and letting die?

  • Rachels' challenge: Active killing (turning off respirator) vs. passive (not starting respirator) - same outcome, why morally different?

  • Personal vs. Impersonal Harm:

  • Contact principle: Direct physical contact (pushing) feels more wrong than remote harm (lever)
  • Psychological distinction: "Up close and personal" violence triggers emotional aversion
  • Evolutionary explanation: Humans evolved strong inhibitions against personal violence
  • Relevance to morality: Is evolutionary psychology a guide to moral truth?

  • Greene's neuroscience: Emotional brain areas activate for personal harm, not impersonal

  • Using Persons as Means:

  • Kantian Formula of Humanity: Treat persons as ends in themselves, never merely as means
  • Lever case: One worker is not used as means (death is side effect of track diversion)
  • Push case: Stranger is used as trolley-stopper (instrumentalized)
  • Organ case: Patient is used as organ source (instrumentalized)

  • Rights-based critique: Five do not have right to one person's body/life

  • Alternative Responses and Critiques:

  • Reject intuitions: Perhaps emotional reactions are unreliable (Unger, Singer)
  • Threshold deontology: Allow exceptions to prohibitions when stakes very high
  • Virtue ethics: What would virtuous person do? (Context-sensitive, no universal rule)
  • Care ethics: Focus on relationships and context, not abstract principles

  • Particularism: No universal moral principles, judgments depend on all features of case

  • Implications and Applications:

  • Autonomous vehicles: Should AV swerve to minimize casualties? (Trolley problem)
  • Medical triage: Allocate scarce resources to save most lives vs. respect rights
  • Warfare: Collateral damage (DDE applied in just war theory)
  • Public policy: Trade-offs between lives (cost-benefit analysis)

  • Experimental philosophy: Survey responses reveal cultural and individual variation

  • Historical and Philosophical Context:

  • Philippa Foot: Introduced trolley problem (1967) to explore DDE
  • Judith Jarvis Thomson: Developed variants (1976, 1985) including footbridge case
  • Thomas Aquinas: Formulated Doctrine of Double Effect (13th century)
  • Immanuel Kant: Categorical Imperative, Formula of Humanity (1785)
  • Bentham & Mill: Utilitarianism (19th century) - consequences matter
  • Frances Kamm: "Trolley Problem Mysteries" (2015) - complex analysis
  • Joshua Greene: Neuroscience of moral judgment (2001+) - dual process theory
  • Peter Singer: Challenges intuitions, defends consequentialism

docs.title: Scenario 3: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
docs.text:
Event Description: Neuroscientists have achieved complete mapping of a human brain's neural activity. They can predict with 99.9% accuracy what a person will report experiencing based on brain states. Given visual cortex activation pattern P1, the person reports seeing "red." Given pattern P2, they report seeing "blue." For any mental state - thoughts, emotions, sensations - there is a corresponding measurable brain state. Despite this predictive success, a philosophical puzzle remains: Why is there subjective experience at all? Why does seeing red feel like something? Why is there "something it is like" to be conscious? Scientists can explain neural correlates of consciousness but not why those neural processes give rise to phenomenal experience (qualia). A philosopher argues: "You've explained the easy problems (how brain processes information, controls behavior) but not the hard problem (why there is subjective experience accompanying those processes)."

Analysis Task: Analyze the hard problem of consciousness and responses from different philosophical positions.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• The Hard Problem Formulation (Chalmers):
  • Easy problems: Explaining cognitive functions (attention, memory, perception, behavior)
    • In principle solvable by neuroscience (mechanistic, computational explanations)
  • Hard problem: Explaining phenomenal consciousness (subjective, first-person experience)
    • Why is there "something it is like" to see red? (Nagel's formulation)
    • Explanatory gap: No obvious bridge from brain states (objective, third-person) to qualia (subjective, first-person)

  • Zombie argument: Conceivable that physical duplicate of person could exist without consciousness (philosophical zombie)

  • Qualia and Phenomenal Consciousness:

  • Qualia: Intrinsic, subjective qualities of experience (redness of red, painfulness of pain)
  • Phenomenal vs. access consciousness: Experience vs. reportability
  • Inverted spectrum: Could my "red" experience be your "green" experience? (Private qualia)
  • Knowledge argument (Jackson): Mary the color scientist knows all physical facts about color but learns something new when she sees red (non-physical fact?)

  • Ineffability: Qualia seem impossible to fully communicate in words

  • Physicalist/Materialist Responses:

  • Identity theory: Mental states are identical to brain states (no explanatory gap)
    • Problem: How can subjective experience be "nothing but" neural firing?
  • Functionalism: Mental states are functional states (defined by causal role, not substrate)
    • Problem: Functional isomorphs (e.g., silicon chips) could have same functions but lack qualia
  • Eliminativism (Churchland): Qualia are illusion, folk psychology will be eliminated
    • Problem: Denying existence of consciousness seems self-refuting

  • Type-B materialism (Block, Carruthers): Gap is epistemic, not metaphysical (we just don't understand yet)

  • Dualist Responses:

  • Substance dualism (Descartes): Mind and matter are distinct substances
    • Problem: Interaction problem (how do immaterial mind and material brain causally interact?)
  • Property dualism (Chalmers): Physical substrate but mental properties are non-physical
    • Qualia as fundamental, irreducible properties of nature (like mass, charge)
    • Avoids interaction problem (properties of same substance)

  • Panpsychism: Consciousness is fundamental, present in all matter (even electrons have proto-experience)

    • Combination problem: How do micro-experiences combine into unified human consciousness?

  • Alternative Frameworks:

  • Mysterianism (McGinn): Humans cognitively closed to understanding consciousness (like dog unable to grasp calculus)
  • Illusionism (Frankish): Phenomenal consciousness is cognitive illusion (we introspect inaccurately)
  • Neutral monism (Russell, James): Mind and matter are two aspects of neutral underlying reality
  • Integrated Information Theory (Tononi): Consciousness is integrated information (Φ) - quantifiable

  • Global Workspace Theory (Baars, Dehaene): Consciousness is global availability of information

  • Methodological and Epistemic Issues:

  • First-person vs. third-person: Science studies third-person data, consciousness is first-person
  • Neurophenomenology: Integrate first-person reports with neuroscience (Varela)
  • Explanatory gap: Does predictive success constitute explanation? (Correlation vs. causation)
  • Conceptual vs. empirical problem: Is hard problem philosophical or scientific?

  • Zombie conceivability: Is conceivability guide to possibility? (Chalmers yes, Dennett no)

  • Implications and Applications:

  • AI consciousness: Could AI have subjective experience? (Functional equivalent but different substrate)
  • Animal consciousness: Do fish, insects, plants have qualia? (Moral implications)
  • Moral status: Is phenomenal consciousness necessary for moral consideration?
  • Mind uploading: If mind transferred to computer, would it be conscious?

  • Anesthesia: What happens to consciousness? (Suspended or absent?)

  • Historical and Philosophical Context:

  • René Descartes: "Meditations" (1641) - mind-body dualism
  • Thomas Nagel: "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" (1974) - subjective character of experience
  • Frank Jackson: "Epiphenomenal Qualia" (1982) - Knowledge argument
  • David Chalmers: "The Conscious Mind" (1996) - formulated hard problem
  • Daniel Dennett: "Consciousness Explained" (1991) - rejects qualia
  • Joseph Levine: "Materialism and qualia: The explanatory gap" (1983)
  • John Searle: Chinese Room argument (1980) - syntax vs. semantics
  • Giulio Tononi: Integrated Information Theory (2000s)

docs.title: Scenario 4: The Gettier Problem and Nature of Knowledge
docs.text:
Event Description: A farmer checks on his sheep in a distant field. He sees a white, fluffy, sheep-shaped object and forms the belief "There is a sheep in the field." Based on this justified, true belief, he reports to his neighbor that his sheep is safe. It turns out: (1) There IS a sheep in the field (true), (2) The farmer is justified in believing this (he saw what looked like a sheep), (3) BUT what he saw was actually a dog covered in wool; the real sheep was hidden behind a rock. So the farmer has justified true belief but seems to lack knowledge. Classical definition of knowledge: Justified True Belief (JTB). Gettier cases challenge this: JTB is not sufficient for knowledge. Another case: Smith believes "Jones owns a Ford OR Brown is in Barcelona" because he has strong evidence Jones owns a Ford (saw him driving it, has title papers). Smith has no idea where Brown is but adds disjunction to make compound statement. It turns out Jones doesn't own a Ford (was borrowing it), but by luck, Brown IS in Barcelona. Smith's belief is true and justified but seems accidental, not knowledge.

Analysis Task: Analyze the Gettier problem and responses attempting to salvage or revise the definition of knowledge.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Classical Justified True Belief (JTB) Account:
  • Three conditions for knowledge: (1) Belief (psychological state), (2) Truth (correspondence to reality), (3) Justification (epistemic grounds)
  • Plato's "Theaetetus": Early formulation (knowledge is true belief with an account/logos)
  • Standard analysis: JTB was consensus definition pre-Gettier (1963)

  • Intuitive appeal: Knowledge requires truth (not falsehood), justification (not lucky guess), and belief (not mere information storage)

  • Gettier's Counterexamples:

  • Sheep/dog case: JTB present, but knowledge absent (lucky that belief is true)
  • Ford/Barcelona case: Justification based on false lemma (Jones owns Ford), conclusion true by accident
  • Structure: Justified belief formed on basis of false evidence, true by luck
  • Epistemic luck: Belief is true not because of justification but by fortunate coincidence

  • General pattern: JTB does not rule out epistemic luck

  • Responses - Adding Fourth Condition:

  • No false lemmas (Clark, Ginet): Justification must not rely on any false intermediary beliefs
    • Sheep case: Belief justified via false lemma "That is a sheep" (really a dog)
    • Problem: What if justification indirectly involves false beliefs? (Infinite regress of checking lemmas)
  • Defeasibility (Lehrer): No true fact that, if added to justification, would defeat it
    • Sheep case: Fact "What farmer saw was a dog" would defeat justification
    • Problem: Complicated to specify which facts are relevant defeaters

  • Causal connection (Goldman): Belief must be caused by the fact that makes it true

    • Sheep case: Belief not caused by actual sheep (caused by dog)
    • Problem: Causal theory has own difficulties (perception, abstract objects)

  • Reliabilism (Goldman):

  • Knowledge requires belief formed by reliable process (high truth-to-belief ratio)
  • Sheep case: Perception is generally reliable, but in this instance produced false belief (dog misidentified)
  • Generality problem: How to specify relevant reference class? (Perception in general? Perception of distant fluffy objects?)

  • New evil demon problem: Reliable processes in demon world don't produce knowledge (truth condition violated)

  • Virtue Epistemology (Sosa, Zagzebski):

  • Knowledge is belief arising from intellectual virtues (abilities, character traits)
  • Animal knowledge (reliabilism) vs. reflective knowledge (understanding one's justification)
  • Sheep case: Farmer's belief doesn't manifest cognitive virtue (perceptual ability undermined by distance/disguise)

  • Advantage: Explains why Gettier cases aren't knowledge (success not due to ability)

  • Contextualism (DeRose, Cohen):

  • "Knowledge" has different standards in different contexts
  • In everyday context, farmer might count as knowing; in skeptical context, no
  • Gettier cases exploit context-shifting intuitions

  • Problem: Seems to relativize knowledge to conversational context (counterintuitive?)

  • Skeptical Response:

  • Gettier problem shows JTB analysis was fundamentally misguided
  • Knowledge may be primitive, unanalyzable concept
  • Or: Knowledge is too context-dependent and interest-relative to admit precise definition

  • Pragmatic shift: Focus on epistemic norms and practices, not definition

  • Implications for Epistemology:

  • Epistemic luck: Problem extends beyond Gettier (lottery cases, environmental luck)
  • Internalism vs. externalism: Must justification be accessible to subject? (Reliability is external)
  • Social epistemology: Testimony, authority, collective knowledge (Gettier cases involve trust)

  • Applied epistemology: Scientific knowledge, legal evidence (standards of justification)

  • Historical and Philosophical Context:

  • Plato: "Theaetetus" (4th century BCE) - JTB account proposed and critiqued
  • Edmund Gettier: "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" (1963) - 3-page paper, revolutionized epistemology
  • Bertrand Russell: Stopped clock case (earlier Gettier-like example)
  • Alvin Goldman: "A Causal Theory of Knowing" (1967) - causal response
  • Ernest Sosa: "The Raft and the Pyramid" (1980) - foundationalism vs. coherentism
  • Keith Lehrer & Thomas Paxson: "Knowledge: Undefeated Justified True Belief" (1969)
  • Timothy Williamson: "Knowledge and Its Limits" (2000) - knowledge as primitive

docs.text:

  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of problem analysis, response evaluation
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear philosophical reasoning, specific theory distinctions

docs.title: Scenario 5: Free Will, Determinism, and Moral Responsibility
docs.text:
Event Description: A person commits a violent crime. Neuroscientists scan their brain and discover abnormalities in the prefrontal cortex (impulse control) and amygdala (emotion regulation) due to childhood trauma and genetic predisposition. The defense attorney argues: "Given the defendant's brain state and history, they could not have done otherwise. Their action was causally determined by prior factors outside their control. Therefore, they are not morally responsible and should not be punished, only treated." The prosecution responds: "Determinism is irrelevant. The defendant had reasons, deliberated, and acted. They are a rational agent capable of responding to incentives. Punishment is justified to deter future crime and hold agents accountable." A compatibilist philosopher testifies: "Free will is compatible with determinism. What matters is whether the person acted according to their own desires and beliefs, free from external coercion. Internal causation by one's own psychology is sufficient for responsibility." A libertarian philosopher counters: "True moral responsibility requires libertarian free will - the ability to have done otherwise in exactly the same circumstances. Without indeterministic agency, we are just sophisticated automatons."

Analysis Task: Analyze the free will debate and its implications for moral responsibility and criminal justice.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Hard Determinism:
  • Thesis: All events (including human actions) are causally determined by prior states and natural laws
  • Incompatibilism: Free will and determinism are incompatible
  • Consequence: No one has free will, no one is morally responsible (in desert-based sense)
  • Arguments: Neuroscience, physics (Laplace's demon), psychological determinism

  • Implication: Retributive punishment unjustified (but may accept consequentialist deterrence)

  • Libertarian Free Will:

  • Thesis: Free will requires indeterminism (agent causation not determined by prior states)
  • Incompatibilism: Agrees with hard determinism that free will and determinism incompatible
  • Assertion: Humans DO have free will (contra hard determinism)
  • Source: Agent causation, quantum indeterminacy in brain, irreducible agency
  • Problem: Randomness (quantum indeterminacy) doesn't seem like control (luck objection)

  • Implication: Moral responsibility requires libertarian free will

  • Compatibilism (Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett):

  • Thesis: Free will is compatible with determinism
  • Free will redefined: Acting according to one's own desires, beliefs, values (internal causation)
  • Unfree: External coercion, compulsion, manipulation (not caused by one's true self)
  • "Could have done otherwise": Hypothetical sense (would have acted differently if desires/beliefs were different)

  • Implication: Moral responsibility compatible with determinism

  • Frankfurt Cases and Hierarchical Views:

  • Harry Frankfurt: Free will is second-order volition (desires about desires)
  • Person acts freely if they identify with their first-order desires
  • Frankfurt case: Alternative possibilities not necessary for responsibility (Black ensures Jones does A, but Jones does A on his own anyway)

  • Hierarchical self: True self vs. alienated desires (addiction, compulsion)

  • Moral Responsibility Conditions:

  • Desert-based: Person deserves praise/blame, punishment/reward
  • Consequentialist: Responsibility attributions are useful for behavior regulation (forward-looking)
  • Strawsonian (reactive attitudes): Responsibility grounded in interpersonal relationships, emotions (resentment, gratitude)

  • Reasons-responsiveness (Fischer & Ravizza): Responsible if agent is responsive to moral reasons

  • Neuroscience and Legal Implications:

  • Brain abnormalities: Prefrontal cortex damage reduces impulse control (Phineas Gage case)
  • Genetic/environmental determinism: Childhood trauma, genes influence behavior
  • Mitigation vs. exculpation: Brain evidence can reduce but not eliminate responsibility?
  • Slippery slope: If brain causes behavior, no one is responsible (hard determinist worry)

  • Pragmatic: Criminal law assumes responsibility, adjusts for diminished capacity

  • Alternative Frameworks:

  • Semi-compatibilism (Fischer): Moral responsibility doesn't require alternative possibilities, but does require reasons-responsiveness
  • Hard incompatibilism (Pereboom): Neither determinism nor indeterminism support moral responsibility
  • Illusionism (Smilansky): Free will is illusion, but necessary illusion for social stability

  • Revisionism: Abandon desert-based responsibility, adopt purely consequentialist justifications for punishment

  • Implications for Criminal Justice:

  • Retributive punishment: Justification undermined if no free will (hard determinist, hard incompatibilist)
  • Deterrence and rehabilitation: Justified on consequentialist grounds (compatible with determinism)
  • Restorative justice: Focus on repair and reconciliation (less reliant on blame)
  • Predictive sentencing: If behavior determined, predict and prevent (but ethical concerns)

  • Responsibility as social construct: Pragmatic tool for social coordination

  • Historical and Philosophical Context:

  • Aristotle: "Nicomachean Ethics" (4th century BCE) - voluntary action
  • David Hume: "Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding" (1748) - compatibilism
  • Immanuel Kant: "Critique of Practical Reason" (1788) - noumenal self, transcendental freedom
  • Pierre-Simon Laplace: Demon thought experiment (1814) - determinism
  • P.F. Strawson: "Freedom and Resentment" (1962) - reactive attitudes
  • Harry Frankfurt: "Freedom of the Will" (1971) - hierarchical account
  • Daniel Dennett: "Elbow Room" (1984) - compatibilism defense
  • Derk Pereboom: "Living Without Free Will" (2001) - hard incompatibilism
  • Benjamin Libet: Neuroscience experiments (1980s) - unconscious initiation of action

docs.title: What High-Quality Analysis Looks Like
docs.text:
Excellent (45-50 points):

  • Applies philosophical concepts and theories accurately (metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, philosophy of mind)
  • Considers multiple philosophical positions and their strengths/weaknesses
  • Makes specific, well-justified philosophical claims with careful argumentation
  • Cites relevant philosophers, texts, and philosophical debates
  • Clear logical structure with premises, inferences, and conclusions
  • Acknowledges objections and responds to counterarguments
  • Identifies subtle conceptual distinctions and implications

Good (35-44 points):

  • Applies key philosophical concepts correctly
  • Considers main philosophical positions on the issue
  • Makes reasonable philosophical claims with supporting arguments
  • References some philosophical literature or major figures
  • Clear reasoning with logical flow
  • Provides useful philosophical insights

Needs Improvement (<35 points):

  • Misapplies philosophical concepts or theories
  • Ignores major philosophical positions or arguments
  • Vague or poorly justified claims
  • Lacks grounding in philosophical literature or tradition
  • Unclear or illogical reasoning
  • Superficial philosophical analysis

docs.title: For Automated Testing (Claude Agent SDK)
docs.text:
from claude_agent_sdk import Agent, TestHarness

agent = Agent.load("philosopher-analyst")
quiz = load_quiz_scenarios("tests/quiz.md")

results = []
for scenario in quiz.scenarios:

    score = evaluate_analysis(analysis, scenario.expected_elements)
    results.append({"scenario": scenario.name, "score": score})

assert sum(r["score"] for r in results) >= 175  # Overall passing
