docs.title: Verification Checklist
docs.text:
Plan and Regulatory Consistency: ☐ Comprehensive plan policies reviewed and applied ☐ Zoning compliance assessed (use, dimensional, design) ☐ State and federal requirements identified ☐ Necessary variances, rezonings, or amendments identified

Impact Assessment: ☐ Transportation impacts quantified (trips, VMT, LOS, multimodal access) ☐ Environmental impacts assessed (stormwater, air, habitat, climate) ☐ Housing impacts analyzed (units, affordability, displacement) ☐ Fiscal impacts calculated (revenues vs. costs) ☐ Community impacts considered (livability, character, services)

Equity Analysis: ☐ Distributional effects identified (who benefits, who is burdened) ☐ Displacement risks assessed and mitigation proposed ☐ Community engagement inclusive and meaningful ☐ Affordable housing and community benefits included ☐ Historical inequities and context considered

Sustainability Assessment: ☐ Greenhouse gas emissions and energy use evaluated ☐ Stormwater management and water quality addressed ☐ Green space and natural resources preserved or enhanced ☐ Climate resilience and adaptation considered ☐ Resource efficiency (water, waste, materials) assessed

Process Quality: ☐ Community and stakeholder engagement documented ☐ Alternatives developed and compared ☐ Data and evidence support conclusions ☐ Implementation feasibility assessed ☐ Monitoring and evaluation framework defined

docs.title: Pitfall 1: Plan-Zoning Inconsistency
docs.text:
Problem: Comprehensive plans envision one future (e.g., walkable mixed-use), but zoning allows another (e.g., single-use, car-oriented), creating contradiction.

Solution: Ensure zoning implements comprehensive plan. Update zoning when plan is adopted or amended. Recognize inconsistency explicitly and plan to resolve it.

docs.title: Pitfall 2: Ignoring Equity and Displacement
docs.text:
Problem: Development or planning initiatives improve an area but displace existing low-income residents and small businesses, particularly communities of color.

Solution: Proactively assess displacement risk. Implement anti-displacement strategies (tenant protections, affordable housing, community land trusts). Center impacted communities in planning. Monitor displacement indicators.

docs.title: Pitfall 3: Overemphasis on Parking
docs.text:
Problem: Requiring excessive parking increases costs, reduces density, encourages driving, creates dead zones, and makes housing less affordable.

Solution: Right-size parking based on actual demand, not outdated standards. Reduce or eliminate minimums, especially near transit. Allow shared parking. Unbundle parking costs from housing. Use parking maximums in some areas.

docs.title: Pitfall 4: Tokenistic Community Engagement
docs.text:
Problem: Checking the box on public participation without meaningfully incorporating community input, building trust, or empowering residents.

Solution: Engage early and often. Go to where people are. Overcome barriers (language, time, childcare). Show how input shaped decisions. Share decision-making power. Compensate community members for expertise.

docs.title: Pitfall 5: Ignoring Fiscal Impacts
docs.text:
Problem: Approving development that seems like "growth" but fiscally unsustainable (especially low-density residential requiring expensive infrastructure extensions).

Solution: Conduct fiscal impact analysis for major decisions. Recognize that compact mixed-use development is typically more fiscally sustainable than sprawl. Consider long-term maintenance costs, not just initial capital.

docs.title: Pitfall 6: Car-Centric Planning
docs.text:
Problem: Designing for vehicle movement and storage as priority, resulting in wide roads, large parking lots, disconnected pedestrian networks, and auto dependence.

Solution: Prioritize people, not cars. Design complete streets for all modes. Emphasize walkability, bikeability, transit access. Reduce road widths, calm traffic. Connect sidewalk networks. Measure success by accessibility, not just traffic speed.

docs.title: Pitfall 7: Neighborhood Character as Exclusion
docs.text:
Problem: Using "neighborhood character" or "compatibility" as coded language to exclude affordable housing, multifamily development, or diverse communities.

Solution: Define character objectively (building form, scale, setbacks) rather than subjectively. Recognize that neighborhoods have always evolved. Question whose vision of "character" is privileged. Balance preservation with growth and inclusion.

docs.title: Pitfall 8: Ignoring Climate Change
docs.text:
Problem: Planning and approving development that increases emissions, exacerbates climate impacts, or fails to prepare for climate risks (flooding, heat, wildfires).

Solution: Evaluate climate impacts of planning decisions. Reduce VMT through land use-transportation coordination. Require green building standards. Protect natural areas. Plan for adaptation and resilience. Avoid development in high-risk areas.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Comprehensive Analysis: ☐ Existing conditions thoroughly documented ☐ Relevant plans, policies, and regulations reviewed ☐ Community context and history understood ☐ Multiple alternatives developed and evaluated ☐ Data and evidence support conclusions

Regulatory Compliance: ☐ Comprehensive plan consistency assessed ☐ Zoning compliance determined ☐ Required approvals identified ☐ State/federal requirements addressed

Impact Assessment: ☐ Transportation, environmental, housing, fiscal, and community impacts quantified ☐ Mitigation measures proposed where needed ☐ Net impacts clearly communicated ☐ Uncertainty acknowledged

Equity and Justice: ☐ Distributional effects analyzed (who wins, who loses) ☐ Displacement risks identified and addressed ☐ Historically marginalized communities centered ☐ Community benefits and affordable housing included ☐ Barriers to participation removed

Sustainability: ☐ Climate impacts assessed and mitigated ☐ Green infrastructure and natural resources prioritized ☐ Walkability and transit access supported ☐ Resource efficiency maximized ☐ Long-term resilience built

Community Engagement: ☐ Diverse stakeholders meaningfully engaged ☐ Input documented and incorporated ☐ Feedback loops established ("here's what we heard") ☐ Trust and relationships built ☐ Decision-making transparent

Implementation: ☐ Specific, actionable recommendations ☐ Implementation actions, timeline, and responsibilities clear ☐ Funding sources and budget identified ☐ Monitoring and evaluation framework established ☐ Political and community support built

docs.title: Integration with Other Analysts
docs.text:
Urban planner analysis complements and integrates with other domain experts:

With Economist: Economic analysis informs development feasibility, fiscal impacts, tax policy, and economic development strategies. Urban planners shape the spatial organization that enables economic activity.

With Environmentalist: Environmental analysis identifies constraints, opportunities, and impacts. Urban planning decisions fundamentally shape environmental outcomes (VMT, stormwater, habitat, emissions).

With Political Scientist: Political analysis explains governance, policy adoption, institutional barriers. Urban planning operates within political systems and requires political will and coalition-building.

With Sociologist: Sociological analysis reveals social structures, inequalities, and community dynamics. Urban planning shapes the physical environment where social life occurs and can reinforce or challenge social patterns.

With Engineer: Engineers design infrastructure systems (transportation, water, sewer, utilities). Urban planners determine where growth occurs and infrastructure is needed, requiring close coordination.

With Historian: Historical analysis provides context on how cities evolved, past planning decisions and their consequences, and historical injustices to be repaired. Urban planning learns from history to avoid repeating mistakes.

What Urban Planner Brings:

  • Spatial thinking and analysis (how location and geography matter)
  • Integration of land use, transportation, environment, housing, economy
  • Long-range perspective (20-30 year horizon)
  • Community engagement and participatory processes
  • Regulatory tools (zoning, comprehensive plans, design standards)
  • Implementation focus (how to achieve goals through concrete actions)

docs.title: Continuous Improvement
docs.text: This skill evolves as urban planning practice advances with new challenges (climate change, housing affordability, equity), new tools (GIS, AI, online engagement platforms), new theories (complexity, resilience, just cities), and lessons from implementation. Document new frameworks, update with recent case studies, incorporate emerging best practices, and refine based on real-world application in diverse planning contexts.

docs.title: Urban Planner Analyst - Domain Validation Quiz
Purpose
docs.text: This quiz validates that the urban planner analyst applies urban planning principles correctly, identifies spatial patterns and infrastructure needs, and provides evidence-based city development analysis. Each scenario requires demonstration of planning frameworks, land use analysis, and sustainable development reasoning.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Transit-Oriented Development Proposal
docs.text:
Event Description: A mid-sized city (population 450,000) plans a new light rail transit (LRT) line connecting the downtown core to a suburban employment hub 12 miles away, with 15 stations. The city proposes rezoning areas within ½ mile of stations from single-family residential to mixed-use, allowing buildings up to 8 stories. The plan anticipates 8,500 new housing units and 12,000 jobs over 15 years. Current residents near proposed stations express concerns about traffic, parking, neighborhood character changes, and gentrification displacing long-term residents. The project requires $2.1 billion in infrastructure investment. Ridership projections estimate 45,000 daily riders by year 10.

Analysis Task: Analyze the transit-oriented development proposal and its urban planning implications.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) Principles:
  • High-density, mixed-use development near transit stations
  • Walkable, pedestrian-oriented design (½ mile = 10-minute walk)
  • Reduced auto dependency and parking requirements
  • Integration of housing, employment, retail, services

  • Support for transit ridership through proximate development

  • Land Use and Zoning Analysis:

  • Current zoning: Single-family residential (low density)
  • Proposed zoning: Mixed-use, 8-story buildings (medium-high density)
  • Density increase: 8,500 housing units (estimate 17,000-21,000 residents)
  • Job-housing balance: 12,000 jobs + residential (reduces commute distances)
  • Floor Area Ratio (FAR) implications

  • Transition zones and height step-downs

  • Transportation Impact Assessment:

  • Mode shift: Projected auto trips reduced by transit use
  • Traffic: Short-term construction disruption, long-term reduction near stations
  • Parking: Reduced requirements (TOD parking ratios lower than suburban)
  • Bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure needs
  • First/last mile connectivity (bus feeders, bike share)

  • Regional congestion mitigation

  • Economic and Fiscal Analysis:

  • Capital cost: $2.1 billion (federal, state, local funding mix)
  • Operating costs: Annual LRT operations and maintenance
  • Property value impacts: Premiums near transit (10-20% typical)
  • Tax revenue: Increased assessed values, development fees
  • Cost-benefit ratio and economic development multipliers

  • Affordability and displacement risks

  • Equity and Gentrification Concerns:

  • Displacement risk: Long-term residents priced out by property value increases
  • Affordability requirements: Inclusionary zoning, affordable housing mandates
  • Anti-displacement strategies: Rent stabilization, community land trusts, tenant protections
  • Equitable development: Benefits distribution, community engagement

  • Environmental justice: Access to opportunity for low-income residents

  • Community Engagement and Opposition:

  • Stakeholder concerns: Traffic, parking, character, displacement
  • NIMBY dynamics: Local opposition to density and change
  • Participatory planning: Community input, co-design processes
  • Addressing concerns: Traffic calming, parking management, design guidelines

  • Building coalitions: Housing advocates, transit users, climate activists

  • Sustainability and Climate Goals:

  • VMT reduction: Vehicle miles traveled decrease (climate benefit)
  • Greenhouse gas emissions: Transportation sector reductions
  • Compact development: Efficient land use, reduced sprawl
  • Green building standards: LEED, net-zero energy

  • Urban heat island mitigation: Green infrastructure, tree canopy

  • Historical Context:

  • Portland, OR: Pioneer in TOD, streetcar and MAX light rail integration
  • Denver RTD FasTracks: Regional rail expansion with TOD zones
  • Arlington, VA Rosslyn-Ballston Corridor: TOD transformation from auto-oriented
  • Minneapolis Hiawatha Line: Gentrification and displacement concerns
  • Research: Transit proximity premiums, ridership-development feedback loops

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct application of TOD principles, land use planning
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of transportation, economic, equity analysis
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear policy recommendations, specific anti-displacement measures
  • Historical Grounding (0-10): References to TOD precedents, research evidence
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from planning goals to implementation to outcomes

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scenario 2: Climate Adaptation Planning
docs.text:
Event Description: A coastal city (population 280,000) faces increasing climate risks: sea level rise projections of 2-3 feet by 2050, intensified hurricanes, and chronic "sunny day" flooding in low-lying neighborhoods. A vulnerability assessment identifies 12,000 residents in flood-prone areas, $4.5 billion in at-risk property, and critical infrastructure (wastewater treatment plant, power substations, hospital) in hazard zones. The city must balance protecting existing development, managing retreat from high-risk areas, and accommodating 15% population growth over 30 years. Funding constraints limit large-scale infrastructure (seawalls cost $10-20 million per mile). Socioeconomic disparities mean low-income communities face highest risk but least capacity to relocate.

Analysis Task: Develop a climate adaptation strategy for the coastal city.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Climate Risk Assessment:
  • Sea level rise: 2-3 feet by 2050 (exponential thereafter)
  • Storm surge: Hurricane intensification, increased flood heights
  • Chronic flooding: King tides, "sunny day" nuisance flooding
  • Exposure: 12,000 residents, $4.5B property, critical infrastructure

  • Timeframe: Near-term (2030), mid-century (2050), long-term (2100)

  • Adaptation Strategy Framework:

  • Protect: Seawalls, levees, floodwalls (high cost, finite protection)
  • Accommodate: Flood-resistant design, elevated structures, wet-proof buildings
  • Retreat: Managed relocation from highest-risk areas
  • Hybrid approach: Risk-based strategies by area

  • Nature-based solutions: Living shorelines, wetland restoration

  • Land Use and Zoning Strategies:

  • Floodplain regulations: Prohibit new development in high-risk zones
  • Overlay districts: Special standards for coastal areas
  • Transfer of development rights (TDR): Incentivize relocation to safer areas
  • Density concentration: Direct growth to inland, higher-elevation areas

  • Rolling easements: Allow natural shoreline migration

  • Infrastructure Resilience:

  • Critical facilities: Relocate or harden (hospital, wastewater plant, power)
  • Transportation: Elevate roads, design for temporary flooding
  • Stormwater management: Green infrastructure, pump stations
  • Utilities: Underground vs. overhead, redundancy

  • Emergency access: Evacuation routes, shelter capacity

  • Managed Retreat and Relocation:

  • Buyout programs: Purchase high-risk properties at fair market value
  • Relocation assistance: Moving costs, down payment support
  • Land banking: Convert bought-out areas to open space, parks
  • Voluntary vs. mandatory programs
  • Destination areas: Affordable housing in safer locations

  • Equity: Ensure low-income residents can afford relocation

  • Equity and Environmental Justice:

  • Disproportionate impacts: Low-income and minority communities in flood zones
  • Capacity to adapt: Financial resources, political influence
  • Affordable housing preservation: Prevent climate gentrification
  • Community engagement: Affected residents in decision-making

  • Just transition: Support for displaced businesses and residents

  • Financing and Implementation:

  • Federal programs: FEMA BRIC, HUD CDBG-DR, Army Corps projects
  • State and local funding: Bonds, resilience taxes, stormwater fees
  • Cost-benefit analysis: Avoided damages vs. adaptation costs
  • Phased implementation: Prioritize highest-risk, critical infrastructure

  • Timeline: 30-year horizon with 5-year action plans

  • Historical Context:

  • New Orleans post-Katrina: Levees, buyouts, population loss
  • Miami Beach: Raised roads, pump stations, "sunny day" flooding
  • NYC post-Sandy: Resilience plans, Build It Back program
  • Staten Island buyouts: Managed retreat from flood-prone areas
  • Norfolk, VA: Recurrent flooding, adaptation planning
  • Research: Climate migration, adaptation limits, maladaptation risks

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct application of adaptation planning, risk assessment frameworks
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of strategy options, equity considerations, financing
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear prioritization, specific relocation and infrastructure measures
  • Historical Grounding (0-10): References to adaptation precedents, climate resilience research
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from risk assessment to strategy selection to implementation

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Scenario 3: Affordable Housing Crisis
docs.text:
Event Description: A rapidly growing tech hub city (population 650,000) faces severe housing affordability challenges. Median home price is $875,000 (up 65% in 5 years), median rent is $2,400/month (up 45%). Cost-burdened households (>30% income on housing) comprise 52% of renters and 35% of owners. Homelessness has increased 38% in 3 years to 4,200 individuals. The jobs-housing imbalance worsens as tech employment grows 8% annually but housing production lags (3,500 units/year vs. 8,000 needed). Long commutes from distant affordable areas strain transportation systems and increase emissions. Neighborhood resistance to new development (especially multi-family) persists despite the crisis.

Analysis Task: Develop a comprehensive affordable housing strategy.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Housing Affordability Assessment:
  • Affordability standard: 30% of income on housing
  • Cost burden: 52% renters, 35% owners exceed threshold
  • Affordability gap: $875K home requires $200K+ income (at 30% threshold)
  • Rental affordability: $2,400/mo requires $96K income
  • Supply-demand imbalance: 8,000 units needed vs. 3,500 produced

  • Job growth outpacing housing: 8% employment vs. housing lag

  • Root Cause Analysis:

  • Supply constraints: Zoning restrictions, development barriers
  • Land use: Single-family zoning limits density (70-80% of residential land typical)
  • Construction costs: Labor, materials, land prices
  • Regulatory barriers: Permitting delays, impact fees, parking requirements
  • NIMBY opposition: Neighborhood resistance to density

  • Speculation and investment: Housing as commodity vs. shelter

  • Zoning and Land Use Reforms:

  • Upzoning: Allow higher density, multi-family in single-family zones
  • Missing middle housing: Duplexes, triplexes, townhomes, courtyard apartments
  • Density bonuses: Extra height/density for affordable units
  • Eliminate exclusionary zoning: Minimum lot sizes, parking mandates
  • Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs): Legalize and streamline

  • Transit-oriented development: High density near transit

  • Affordable Housing Production:

  • Inclusionary zoning: Require percentage of affordable units in new development
  • Public housing: Direct government construction and management
  • Social housing: Non-profit, cooperative, community land trust models
  • Subsidies: Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), project-based vouchers
  • Density bonus programs: Developer incentives for affordability

  • Target: 30% of new units at 60-80% AMI, 10% at 30-50% AMI

  • Anti-Displacement and Preservation:

  • Rent stabilization: Limit rent increases in existing units
  • Tenant protections: Just cause eviction, relocation assistance
  • Acquisition and preservation: Purchase at-risk affordable housing
  • Community land trusts: Permanent affordability through ground leases

  • Affordable housing overlay zones: Protect existing affordable areas

  • Addressing Homelessness:

  • Housing First approach: Rapid rehousing without preconditions
  • Supportive housing: Permanent housing + services for chronically homeless
  • Emergency shelter: Immediate capacity expansion
  • Prevention: Rental assistance, eviction prevention programs
  • Coordinated entry: Centralized assessment and resource allocation

  • Scale: 4,200 individuals need pathways to housing

  • Financing and Revenue:

  • Affordable housing bonds: Voter-approved debt for production
  • Linkage fees: Commercial development fees for housing fund
  • Real estate transfer taxes: Revenue from property sales
  • Land value capture: Tax increment financing in upzoned areas
  • Federal and state funding: HOME, CDBG, state housing trust funds

  • Public land: Surplus public sites for affordable housing

  • Regional Coordination:

  • Jobs-housing balance: Employment centers provide or fund housing
  • Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA): Allocation of growth targets
  • Fair share: Suburban jurisdictions accept affordable housing

  • Transportation-housing coordination: Transit investments with housing

  • Historical Context:

  • Vienna social housing: 60% of residents in public/social housing
  • Minneapolis zoning reform (2018): Legalized triplexes citywide
  • Oregon statewide duplex law (2019): Mandate middle housing
  • California SB 9 and 10: State-level zoning reforms
  • Seattle HALA (2015): Upzoning and affordable housing production
  • Research: Filtering theory, supply elasticity, inclusionary zoning effectiveness

docs.title: Scenario 4: Post-Industrial Neighborhood Revitalization
docs.text:
Event Description: A former manufacturing district (450 acres, 3,200 residents) has been economically depressed for 30 years following factory closures. Current conditions: 35% vacancy rate in commercial buildings, median household income 40% below city average, unemployment 12% (vs. 5% citywide), aging housing stock in disrepair, contaminated brownfield sites (12 parcels), limited retail and services, high crime rates, underperforming schools. The city has designated the area as a redevelopment zone with tax increment financing, streamlined permitting, and infrastructure investments planned. Private developers express interest in mixed-use projects, but residents fear gentrification and displacement. Community organizations demand local hiring, affordable housing, and preservation of neighborhood character.

Analysis Task: Develop an equitable neighborhood revitalization plan.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Neighborhood Assessment:
  • Physical: 35% vacancy, brownfields, aging housing, infrastructure deficits
  • Economic: Low income (40% below city), 12% unemployment, limited retail
  • Social: High crime, underperforming schools, social isolation
  • Assets: Historic architecture, proximity to downtown, engaged community

  • Opportunity: Redevelopment potential, market interest, public investment

  • Revitalization Goals and Trade-offs:

  • Economic development vs. affordability
  • New investment vs. displacement of existing residents
  • Physical improvement vs. cultural preservation
  • Market-rate development vs. subsidized housing

  • Balancing competing interests: Developers, residents, city

  • Brownfield Remediation and Reuse:

  • Environmental assessment and cleanup (12 contaminated parcels)
  • Funding: EPA Brownfield Grants, state programs, developer contributions
  • Reuse planning: Mixed-use, parks, stormwater management
  • Liability protections: Voluntary cleanup programs, environmental covenants

  • Timeline and phasing: Cleanup precedes development

  • Land Use and Redevelopment Strategy:

  • Mixed-use zoning: Residential, commercial, light industrial, maker spaces
  • Adaptive reuse: Convert vacant industrial buildings to housing, retail, offices
  • Infill development: New construction on vacant parcels
  • Historic preservation: Retain character-defining features

  • Green infrastructure: Stormwater parks, green streets, urban agriculture

  • Affordable Housing and Anti-Displacement:

  • Inclusionary requirements: 25-30% affordable in new development
  • Existing housing rehabilitation: Preserve affordable units
  • Community land trusts: Permanent affordability mechanism
  • Tenant protections: Anti-displacement vouchers, relocation assistance

  • Target: No net loss of affordable units, increase affordable supply

  • Economic Development and Job Creation:

  • Local hiring mandates: Construction jobs (30-40%), permanent jobs (20-30%)
  • Workforce development: Training programs for neighborhood residents
  • Small business support: Technical assistance, low-interest loans, below-market rent
  • Retail and services: Grocery store, healthcare, childcare (reduce neighborhood services gap)

  • Living wage requirements: Ensure jobs lift families out of poverty

  • Community Engagement and Governance:

  • Participatory planning: Resident-led visioning and design
  • Community benefits agreement (CBA): Legally binding developer commitments
  • Ongoing oversight: Community advisory board, development review
  • Transparent decision-making: Public data, accessible meetings

  • Build trust: Address historical disinvestment and broken promises

  • Financing and Incentives:

  • Tax Increment Financing (TIF): Capture increased property tax revenue
  • Opportunity Zones: Federal tax incentives (monitor for equity outcomes)
  • New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC): Investment in low-income communities
  • Public infrastructure: Streets, utilities, parks (catalyze private investment)

  • Phasing: Public investment first, then private development

  • Historical Context:

  • Pittsburgh Strip District: Industrial to mixed-use, some displacement
  • Atlanta BeltLine: Rail-to-trail, TOD, gentrification concerns, CBA
  • Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative (Boston): Community land trust, resident control
  • San Francisco Mission District: Gentrification resistance, anti-displacement measures
  • Buffalo waterfront revitalization: Brownfield cleanup, public access
  • Research: Gentrification patterns, anti-displacement strategies, TIF effectiveness

  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of equity strategies, economic development, community engagement
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear anti-displacement measures, specific local hiring and affordability targets
  • Historical Grounding (0-10): References to revitalization precedents, equity research

docs.title: Scenario 5: Regional Growth Management
docs.text:
Event Description: A metropolitan region (1.8 million population, 5 counties, 42 municipalities) faces uncoordinated sprawl development. Over 20 years, population grew 35% but urbanized land increased 65% (low-density suburban expansion). Consequences include: VMT increased 48% (traffic congestion, emissions), agricultural land loss (45,000 acres converted), infrastructure costs ($8 billion in roads, water, sewer for dispersed development), school overcrowding in suburbs, job-housing imbalance (long commutes), and environmental impacts (habitat fragmentation, water quality degradation). The region's core cities experience population decline, vacant properties, and declining tax bases while suburbs resist affordable housing and transit.

Analysis Task: Develop a regional growth management framework.

docs.title: Expected Analysis Elements
docs.text:
• Sprawl Assessment and Impacts:
  • Sprawl pattern: 35% population growth, 65% land consumption (inefficient)
  • Transportation: 48% VMT increase, congestion, emissions
  • Fiscal: $8B infrastructure costs for dispersed development
  • Environmental: 45,000 acres farmland lost, habitat fragmentation, water quality
  • Social: Segregation by income and race, job-housing imbalance, long commutes

  • Equity: Suburban exclusion of affordable housing, core city disinvestment

  • Regional Governance Challenges:

  • Fragmentation: 42 municipalities, competing interests
  • Race to the bottom: Jurisdictions compete for tax base, resist affordable housing
  • Coordination failures: No mechanism for regional decisions
  • State vs. local: Home rule traditions, resistance to state mandates

  • Incentive misalignment: Municipalities benefit from growth, externalize costs

  • Growth Management Strategies:

  • Urban Growth Boundaries (UGBs): Contain urban expansion, direct infill
  • Regional plans: Coordinated land use, transportation, housing
  • Infill and redevelopment: Prioritize core cities and inner suburbs
  • Agricultural preservation: Purchase development rights, ag zoning
  • Green infrastructure: Regional trail networks, habitat corridors

  • Performance standards: Density minimums, VMT targets, affordable housing quotas

  • Regional Transportation-Land Use Integration:

  • Transit investments: Regional rail, bus rapid transit in dense corridors
  • TOD around stations: Coordinated zoning and housing targets
  • Complete streets: Walkable, bikeable neighborhoods
  • VMT reduction goals: 20-30% per capita by 2040
  • Congestion pricing: Disincentivize driving, fund transit

  • Parking policies: Reduce minimums, price on-street parking

  • Fair Share Affordable Housing:

  • Regional Housing Needs Assessment: Allocate housing targets by jurisdiction
  • Affordable housing mandates: All jurisdictions accept fair share
  • Enforcement mechanisms: State override of exclusionary zoning, funding penalties
  • Funding pooling: Regional housing trust fund, cross-subsidies

  • Target: 20-25% of regional housing at affordable levels

  • Infrastructure and Service Efficiency:

  • Compact development: Lower per-capita infrastructure costs
  • Shared services: Regional water, transit, waste management
  • Fiscal impact analysis: Full-cost accounting for sprawl vs. infill
  • Green infrastructure: Natural stormwater management vs. grey infrastructure

  • School planning: Coordinate land use and education capacity

  • Environmental Protection:

  • Critical habitat: No-development zones, conservation easements
  • Farmland preservation: Ag districts, differential tax assessment
  • Water quality: Source water protection, watershed management
  • Climate mitigation: Compact development reduces emissions

  • Ecosystem services: Maintain forests, wetlands, floodplains

  • Governance Models and Tools:

  • Metropolitan Planning Organization (MPO): Transportation and land use coordination
  • Regional councils: Voluntary coordination (weak) or binding authority (strong)
  • State mandates: Growth management requirements (OR, WA, MD models)
  • Tax-base sharing: Minnesota Fiscal Disparities model

  • Regulatory tools: State zoning overrides, regional permits

  • Historical Context:

  • Portland Metro: UGB, regional planning authority, transit-land use integration
  • Minneapolis-St. Paul: Fiscal disparities tax-base sharing (1971)
  • Oregon statewide land use planning (1973): UGBs, agricultural preservation
  • Maryland Smart Growth (1997): Priority Funding Areas, rural preservation
  • New Jersey State Plan: Cross-acceptance process, growth tiers
  • Research: Sprawl costs, compact development benefits, regional governance effectiveness

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
• Domain Accuracy (0-10): Correct application of growth management, regional planning principles
  • Analytical Depth (0-10): Thoroughness of sprawl impacts, governance strategies, implementation tools
  • Insight Specificity (0-10): Clear regional coordination mechanisms, specific growth management policies
  • Historical Grounding (0-10): References to regional planning precedents, research evidence
  • Reasoning Clarity (0-10): Logical flow from sprawl diagnosis to regional coordination to implementation

Minimum Passing Score: 35/50

docs.title: Complexity Estimation Algorithm
docs.text:
def estimate_complexity(item: dict) -> str:
    hours = item.get("estimated_hours", 4)

    # Base complexity
    if hours < 2:
        base = "simple"
    elif hours <= 6:
        base = "medium"
    else:
        base = "complex"

    # Adjust for technical signals
    text = item["title"] + " " + item["description"]
    signals = {
        "api_changes": "api" in text or "endpoint" in text,
        "db_changes": "database" in text or "schema" in text,
        "ui_changes": "ui" in text or "frontend" in text,
        "security": "auth" in text or "security" in text
    }

    complexity_count = sum(signals.values())

    # Increase complexity if 3+ technical signals
    if complexity_count >= 3:
        if base == "simple":
            base = "medium"
        elif base == "medium":
            base = "complex"

    return base

docs.title: File Discovery Strategy
docs.text:

  2. Path search: Search common locations (src/, tests/, .claude/tools/)
  3. Filename matching: Match keywords against file/directory names
  4. Limit: Return top 10 most relevant files

Example:

Item: "Implement config parser"
Keywords: ["implement", "config", "parser"]

Search paths:
- src/config/ → config.py, parser.py
- tests/ → test_config.py
- .claude/tools/ → (none)

Relevant files (3 found):
1. src/config/loader.py (matches "config")
2. tests/test_config.py (matches "config", "test")
3. src/utils/parser_base.py (matches "parser")

docs.title: Coordination Algorithm
docs.text:
def coordinate(project_root):
    # Load workstreams
    workstreams = load_all_workstreams(project_root)

    # Categorize by status
    active = [ws for ws in workstreams if ws.status == "RUNNING"]
    paused = [ws for ws in workstreams if ws.status == "PAUSED"]
    completed = [ws for ws in workstreams if ws.status == "COMPLETED"]

    # Detect issues
    stalled = detect_stalled(active, threshold_hours=2)
    conflicts = detect_conflicts(active, backlog_items)

    # Analyze capacity
    capacity = analyze_capacity(len(active), max_concurrent=5)

    # Generate recommendations
    recommendations = []
    if stalled:
        recommendations.append(f"Investigate {len(stalled)} stalled workstream(s)")
    if conflicts:
        recommendations.append(f"Resolve {len(conflicts)} dependency conflict(s)")
    if capacity.utilization > 80:
        recommendations.append("High capacity - prioritize completion")
    if len(active) == 0 and ready_items > 0:
        recommendations.append(f"No active work - {ready_items} items ready")

    return {
        "active": active,
        "stalled": stalled,
        "conflicts": conflicts,
        "capacity": capacity,
        "recommendations": recommendations
    }

docs.title: Stall Detection Logic
docs.text:
def detect_stalled(workstreams, threshold_hours=2):
    stalled = []
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    for ws in workstreams:
        if ws.status != "RUNNING":
            continue

        last_activity = parse_timestamp(ws.last_activity)
        idle_hours = (now - last_activity).total_seconds() / 3600

        if idle_hours > threshold_hours:
            stalled.append({
                "workstream": ws.id,
                "title": ws.title,
                "idle_hours": round(idle_hours, 1),
                "recommendation": "Investigate or pause"
            })

    return stalled

docs.title: Conflict Detection Logic
docs.text:
def detect_conflicts(workstreams, backlog_items):
    conflicts = []

    # Build dependency map
    item_deps = {item.id: item.dependencies for item in backlog_items}

    # Check each active workstream
    for ws in workstreams:
        if ws.status != "RUNNING":
            continue

        deps = item_deps.get(ws.backlog_id, [])

        # Check if any dependency is also active
        for other_ws in workstreams:
            if other_ws.id == ws.id:
                continue

            if other_ws.status == "RUNNING" and other_ws.backlog_id in deps:
                conflicts.append({
                    "type": "dependency",
                    "workstream": ws.id,
                    "depends_on": other_ws.id,
                    "reason": f"{ws.id} depends on {other_ws.backlog_id} in progress"
                })

    return conflicts

docs.title: Zero-Error Requirement
docs.text:
All Excel files created with this skill MUST have zero formula errors. The recalc.py script verifies:

  • #REF! - Invalid cell references
  • #DIV/0! - Division by zero
  • #VALUE! - Wrong data type in formula
  • #NAME? - Unrecognized formula name
  • #NULL! - Incorrect range operator
  • #NUM! - Invalid numeric value
  • #N/A - Value not available

If errors are found, the script reports their locations and counts for correction.

docs.text:

Untrusted Excel Files: When opening Excel files from untrusted sources, be aware that openpyxl does not execute VBA macros, but malicious formulas could still be present. Use the recalc.py script to verify zero formula errors.

docs.title: Industry-Standard Color Conventions
docs.text:
• Blue text (RGB: 0,0,255): Hardcoded inputs, and numbers users will change for scenarios
  • Black text (RGB: 0,0,0): ALL formulas and calculations
  • Green text (RGB: 0,128,0): Links pulling from other worksheets within same workbook
  • Red text (RGB: 255,0,0): External links to other files
  • Yellow background (RGB: 255,255,0): Key assumptions needing attention or cells that need to be updated

docs.title: Required Format Rules
docs.text:
• Years: Format as text strings (e.g., "2024" not "2,024")
  • Currency: Use \(#,##0 format; ALWAYS specify units in headers ("Revenue (\)mm)")
  • Zeros: Use number formatting to make all zeros "-", including percentages (e.g., "\(#,##0;(\)#,##0);-")
  • Percentages: Default to 0.0% format (one decimal)
  • Multiples: Format as 0.0x for valuation multiples (EV/EBITDA, P/E)
  • Negative numbers: Use parentheses (123) not minus -123

docs.title: Assumptions Placement
docs.text:
• Place ALL assumptions (growth rates, margins, multiples, etc.) in separate assumption cells
  • Use cell references instead of hardcoded values in formulas
  • Example: Use =B5*(1+\(B\)6) instead of =B5*1.05

docs.title: Formula Error Prevention
docs.text:
• Verify all cell references are correct
  • Check for off-by-one errors in ranges
  • Ensure consistent formulas across all projection periods
  • Test with edge cases (zero values, negative numbers)
  • Verify no unintended circular references

docs.title: Documentation Requirements for Hardcodes
docs.text:
• Comment or in cells beside (if end of table). Format: "Source: [System/Document], [Date], [Specific Reference], [URL if applicable]"
  • Examples:
  • "Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]"
  • "Source: Company 10-Q, Q2 2025, Exhibit 99.1, [SEC EDGAR URL]"
  • "Source: Bloomberg Terminal, 8/15/2025, AAPL US Equity"
  • "Source: FactSet, 8/20/2025, Consensus Estimates Screen"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A user may ask you to create, edit, or analyze the contents of an .xlsx file. You have different tools and workflows available for different tasks.

docs.title: Important Requirements
docs.text: LibreOffice Required for Formula Recalculation: You can assume LibreOffice is installed for recalculating formula values using the recalc.py script. The script automatically configures LibreOffice on first run

docs.title: Data analysis with pandas
docs.text:
For data analysis, visualization, and basic operations, use pandas which provides powerful data manipulation capabilities:

import pandas as pd

# Read Excel
df = pd.read_excel('file.xlsx')  # Default: first sheet
all_sheets = pd.read_excel('file.xlsx', sheet_name=None)  # All sheets as dict

# Analyze
df.head()      # Preview data
df.info()      # Column info
df.describe()  # Statistics

# Write Excel
df.to_excel('output.xlsx', index=False)

docs.title: CRITICAL: Use Formulas, Not Hardcoded Values
docs.text: Always use Excel formulas instead of calculating values in Python and hardcoding them. This ensures the spreadsheet remains dynamic and updateable.

docs.title: ❌ WRONG - Hardcoding Calculated Values
docs.text:
# Bad: Calculating in Python and hardcoding result
total = df['Sales'].sum()
sheet['B10'] = total  # Hardcodes 5000

# Bad: Computing growth rate in Python
growth = (df.iloc[-1]['Revenue'] - df.iloc[0]['Revenue']) / df.iloc[0]['Revenue']
sheet['C5'] = growth  # Hardcodes 0.15

# Bad: Python calculation for average
avg = sum(values) / len(values)
sheet['D20'] = avg  # Hardcodes 42.5

docs.title: ✅ CORRECT - Using Excel Formulas
docs.text:
# Good: Let Excel calculate the sum
sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'

# Good: Growth rate as Excel formula
sheet['C5'] = '=(C4-C2)/C2'

# Good: Average using Excel function
sheet['D20'] = '=AVERAGE(D2:D19)'

This applies to ALL calculations - totals, percentages, ratios, differences, etc. The spreadsheet should be able to recalculate when source data changes.

docs.title: Common Workflow
docs.text:
1. Choose tool: pandas for data, openpyxl for formulas/formatting
  2. Create/Load: Create new workbook or load existing file
  3. Modify: Add/edit data, formulas, and formatting
  4. Save: Write to file
  5. Recalculate formulas (MANDATORY IF USING FORMULAS): Use the recalc.py script 
    python recalc.py output.xlsx
  6. Verify and fix any errors:
  7. The script returns JSON with error details
  8. If status is errors_found, check error_summary for specific error types and locations
  9. Fix the identified errors and recalculate again
  10. Common errors to fix:
    • #REF!: Invalid cell references
    • #DIV/0!: Division by zero
    • #VALUE!: Wrong data type in formula
    • #NAME?: Unrecognized formula name

docs.title: Creating new Excel files
docs.text:
# Using openpyxl for formulas and formatting
from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font, PatternFill, Alignment

wb = Workbook()
sheet = wb.active

# Add data
sheet['A1'] = 'Hello'
sheet['B1'] = 'World'
sheet.append(['Row', 'of', 'data'])

# Add formula
sheet['B2'] = '=SUM(A1:A10)'

# Formatting
sheet['A1'].font = Font(bold=True, color='FF0000')
sheet['A1'].fill = PatternFill('solid', start_color='FFFF00')
sheet['A1'].alignment = Alignment(horizontal='center')

# Column width
sheet.column_dimensions['A'].width = 20

wb.save('output.xlsx')

docs.title: Editing existing Excel files
docs.text:
# Using openpyxl to preserve formulas and formatting
from openpyxl import load_workbook

# Load existing file
wb = load_workbook('existing.xlsx')
sheet = wb.active  # or wb['SheetName'] for specific sheet

# Working with multiple sheets
for sheet_name in wb.sheetnames:
    sheet = wb[sheet_name]
    print(f"Sheet: {sheet_name}")

# Modify cells
sheet['A1'] = 'New Value'
sheet.insert_rows(2)  # Insert row at position 2
sheet.delete_cols(3)  # Delete column 3

# Add new sheet
new_sheet = wb.create_sheet('NewSheet')
new_sheet['A1'] = 'Data'

wb.save('modified.xlsx')

docs.title: Recalculating formulas
docs.text:
Excel files created or modified by openpyxl contain formulas as strings but not calculated values. Use the provided recalc.py script to recalculate formulas:

python recalc.py <excel_file> [timeout_seconds]

Example:

python recalc.py output.xlsx 30

The script:

  • Automatically sets up LibreOffice macro on first run
  • Recalculates all formulas in all sheets
  • Scans ALL cells for Excel errors (#REF!, #DIV/0!, etc.)
  • Returns JSON with detailed error locations and counts
  • Works on both Linux and macOS

docs.title: Formula Verification Checklist
docs.text: Quick checks to ensure formulas work correctly:

docs.title: Essential Verification
docs.text:
• Test 2-3 sample references: Verify they pull correct values before building full model
  • Column mapping: Confirm Excel columns match (e.g., column 64 = BL, not BK)
  • Row offset: Remember Excel rows are 1-indexed (DataFrame row 5 = Excel row 6)

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
• NaN handling: Check for null values with pd.notna()
  • Far-right columns: FY data often in columns 50+
  • Multiple matches: Search all occurrences, not just first
  • Division by zero: Check denominators before using / in formulas (#DIV/0!)
  • Wrong references: Verify all cell references point to intended cells (#REF!)
  • Cross-sheet references: Use correct format (Sheet1!A1) for linking sheets

docs.title: Formula Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Start small: Test formulas on 2-3 cells before applying broadly
  • Verify dependencies: Check all cells referenced in formulas exist
  • Test edge cases: Include zero, negative, and very large values

docs.title: Interpreting recalc.py Output
docs.text:
The script returns JSON with error details:

{
  "status": "success", // or "errors_found"
  "total_errors": 0, // Total error count
  "total_formulas": 42, // Number of formulas in file
  "error_summary": {
    // Only present if errors found
    "#REF!": {
      "count": 2,
      "locations": ["Sheet1!B5", "Sheet1!C10"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Library Selection
docs.text:
• pandas: Best for data analysis, bulk operations, and simple data export
  • openpyxl: Best for complex formatting, formulas, and Excel-specific features

docs.title: Working with openpyxl
docs.text:
• Cell indices are 1-based (row=1, column=1 refers to cell A1)
  • Use data_only=True to read calculated values: load_workbook('file.xlsx', data_only=True)
  • Warning: If opened with data_only=True and saved, formulas are replaced with values and permanently lost
  • For large files: Use read_only=True for reading or write_only=True for writing
  • Formulas are preserved but not evaluated - use recalc.py to update values

docs.title: Working with pandas
docs.text:
• Specify data types to avoid inference issues: pd.read_excel('file.xlsx', dtype={'id': str})
  • For large files, read specific columns: pd.read_excel('file.xlsx', usecols=['A', 'C', 'E'])
  • Handle dates properly: pd.read_excel('file.xlsx', parse_dates=['date_column'])

docs.title: Code Style Guidelines
docs.text:
IMPORTANT: When generating Python code for Excel operations:

  • Write minimal, concise Python code without unnecessary comments
  • Avoid verbose variable names and redundant operations
  • Avoid unnecessary print statements

For Excel files themselves:

  • Add comments to cells with complex formulas or important assumptions
  • Document data sources for hardcoded values
  • Include notes for key calculations and model sections

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Spreadsheet Creation

Task: Create a simple expense tracker with totals.

User Request: "Create an Excel file tracking my monthly expenses with categories and totals."

Implementation:

from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font, PatternFill

wb = Workbook()

sheet.title = "Expenses"

# Headers
sheet['A1'] = 'Category'
sheet['B1'] = 'Amount'
sheet['A1'].font = Font(bold=True)
sheet['B1'].font = Font(bold=True)

# Data
expenses = [
    ('Rent', 1200),
    ('Groceries', 400),
    ('Utilities', 150),
    ('Transportation', 200)
]

row = 2
for category, amount in expenses:
    sheet[f'A{row}'] = category
    sheet[f'B{row}'] = amount
    row += 1

# Total row with formula
sheet[f'A{row}'] = 'Total'
sheet[f'B{row}'] = f'=SUM(B2:B{row-1})'  # Formula, not hardcoded
sheet[f'A{row}'].font = Font(bold=True)
sheet[f'B{row}'].font = Font(bold=True)

docs.title: Example 3: Data Analysis with pandas
docs.text:
Task: Analyze sales data and create summary statistics.

User Request: "Load sales data from CSV and create an Excel report with statistics."

Implementation:

import pandas as pd

# Sample data (in practice, load from CSV)
data = {
    'Product': ['Widget A', 'Widget B', 'Widget C'] * 12,
    'Month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun',
              'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct', 'Nov', 'Dec'] * 3,
    'Sales': [5000, 5200, 4800, 5500, 6000, 6200,
              6500, 6100, 5900, 6300, 6700, 7000,
              3000, 3100, 2900, 3200, 3400, 3500,
              3600, 3300, 3200, 3500, 3700, 3800]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# Calculate summary statistics
summary = df.groupby('Product')['Sales'].agg([
    ('Total Sales', 'sum'),
    ('Average', 'mean'),
    ('Min', 'min'),
    ('Max', 'max')
]).reset_index()

# Create Excel file with multiple sheets
with pd.ExcelWriter('sales_analysis.xlsx', engine='openpyxl') as writer:
    df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name='Raw Data', index=False)
    summary.to_excel(writer, sheet_name='Summary', index=False)

print("Sales analysis created: sales_analysis.xlsx")

Result: Multi-sheet Excel workbook with raw data and summary statistics.

docs.title: Example 5: Multi-Year Budget Model
docs.text:
Task: Create a detailed budget with multiple categories over 3 years.

User Request: "Build a budget model for my business with quarterly breakdown for 3 years."

Implementation:

from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font, Alignment

wb = Workbook()
sheet = wb.active
sheet.title = "Budget Model"

# Headers
sheet['A1'] = 'Budget Model 2024-2026'
sheet['A1'].font = Font(bold=True, size=14)

# Time periods
periods = ['Q1 2024', 'Q2 2024', 'Q3 2024', 'Q4 2024',
           'Q1 2025', 'Q2 2025', 'Q3 2025', 'Q4 2025',
           'Q1 2026', 'Q2 2026', 'Q3 2026', 'Q4 2026']

sheet['A3'] = 'Category'
for idx, period in enumerate(periods, start=2):
    cell = sheet.cell(3, idx, period)
    cell.font = Font(bold=True)
    cell.alignment = Alignment(horizontal='center')

# Budget categories with formulas
categories = {
    'Revenue': 100000,
    'Cost of Sales': -40000,
    'Salaries': -30000,
    'Rent': -5000,
    'Marketing': -8000,
    'Utilities': -2000
}

row = 4
for category, base_amount in categories.items():
    sheet.cell(row, 1, category)
    sheet.cell(row, 1).font = Font(bold=category == 'Revenue')

    # Q1 2024 - base value
    sheet.cell(row, 2, base_amount)
    sheet.cell(row, 2).font = Font(color='0000FF')  # Blue input
    sheet.cell(row, 2).number_format = '$#,##0;($#,##0);-'

    # Subsequent quarters - growth formula (2% per quarter)
    for col in range(3, 14):
        prev_col = chr(ord('A') + col - 2)
        sheet.cell(row, col, f'={prev_col}{row}*1.02')  # 2% growth
        sheet.cell(row, col).font = Font(color='000000')  # Black formula
        sheet.cell(row, col).number_format = '$#,##0;($#,##0);-'

    row += 1

# Net Income row
sheet.cell(row, 1, 'Net Income')
sheet.cell(row, 1).font = Font(bold=True)
for col in range(2, 14):
    col_letter = chr(ord('A') + col - 1)
    sheet.cell(row, col, f'=SUM({col_letter}4:{col_letter}{row-1})')
    sheet.cell(row, col).font = Font(bold=True, color='000000')
    sheet.cell(row, col).number_format = '$#,##0'

# Set column widths
sheet.column_dimensions['A'].width = 20
for col in range(2, 14):
    sheet.column_dimensions[chr(ord('A') + col - 1)].width = 12

wb.save('budget_model.xlsx')

Recalculate:

python .claude/skills/xlsx/scripts/recalc.py budget_model.xlsx

Result: Comprehensive budget model with quarterly projections and automatic totals.

docs.title: Example 8: Data Import and Transformation
docs.text:
Task: Load messy data, clean it, and export to Excel.

User Request: "Clean this sales data and create a professional Excel report."

Implementation:

import pandas as pd
from openpyxl import load_workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font

# Sample messy data
raw_data = {
    'customer_name': ['  John Doe', 'Jane Smith  ', 'Bob Jones', None, 'Alice Brown'],
    'order_date': ['2024-01-15', '2024-01-20', 'invalid', '2024-02-01', '2024-02-15'],
    'amount': ['1000', '1500.50', 'invalid', '2000', '750.25']
}

df = pd.DataFrame(raw_data)

# Clean data
df['customer_name'] = df['customer_name'].str.strip()  # Remove whitespace
df = df.dropna(subset=['customer_name'])  # Remove null customers
df['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_date'], errors='coerce')  # Parse dates
df = df.dropna(subset=['order_date'])  # Remove invalid dates
df['amount'] = pd.to_numeric(df['amount'], errors='coerce')  # Parse amounts
df = df.dropna(subset=['amount'])  # Remove invalid amounts

# Calculate summary
summary = {
    'Total Orders': len(df),
    'Total Revenue': df['amount'].sum(),
    'Average Order': df['amount'].mean()
}

# Export to Excel with pandas
with pd.ExcelWriter('sales_report.xlsx', engine='openpyxl') as writer:
    df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name='Clean Data', index=False)

    # Summary sheet
    summary_df = pd.DataFrame(list(summary.items()), columns=['Metric', 'Value'])
    summary_df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name='Summary', index=False)

# Post-process with openpyxl for formatting
wb = load_workbook('sales_report.xlsx')

# Format Summary sheet
summary_sheet = wb['Summary']
summary_sheet['A1'].font = Font(bold=True)
summary_sheet['B1'].font = Font(bold=True)
summary_sheet['B2'].number_format = '0'
summary_sheet['B3'].number_format = '$#,##0.00'
summary_sheet['B4'].number_format = '$#,##0.00'

wb.save('sales_report.xlsx')

Result: Clean data and formatted summary report in Excel.

docs.title: Example 9: Formula Error Detection
docs.text:
Task: Create a spreadsheet with formulas and verify zero errors.

User Request: "Build a spreadsheet and make sure all formulas calculate correctly."

Implementation:

from openpyxl import Workbook
import subprocess
import json

wb = Workbook()
sheet = wb.active

# Create some formulas
sheet['A1'] = 'Value 1'
sheet['B1'] = 100
sheet['A2'] = 'Value 2'
sheet['B2'] = 200
sheet['A3'] = 'Total'
sheet['B3'] = '=SUM(B1:B2)'

sheet['A5'] = 'Average'
sheet['B5'] = '=AVERAGE(B1:B2)'

sheet['A7'] = 'Percentage'
sheet['B7'] = '=B1/B3'
sheet['B7'].number_format = '0.0%'

wb.save('formulas_test.xlsx')

# Recalculate and verify
result = subprocess.run(
    ['python', '.claude/skills/xlsx/scripts/recalc.py', 'formulas_test.xlsx'],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True
)

# Parse result
verification = json.loads(result.stdout)

if verification['status'] == 'success':
    print(f"✓ Success! All {verification['total_formulas']} formulas calculated correctly.")
else:
    print(f"✗ Found {verification['total_errors']} errors:")
    for error_type, details in verification['error_summary'].items():
        print(f"  {error_type}: {details['count']} errors")
        for location in details['locations']:
            print(f"    - {location}")

Result: Spreadsheet with verified formulas and detailed error reporting if any issues found.

docs.title: Example 10: Multi-Sheet Financial Model
docs.text:
Task: Create a comprehensive financial model with multiple linked sheets.

User Request: "Build a complete financial model with separate sheets for assumptions, income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow."

Implementation:

from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.styles import Font, PatternFill

wb = Workbook()

# Remove default sheet
wb.remove(wb.active)

# Sheet 1: Assumptions
assumptions = wb.create_sheet("Assumptions")
assumptions['A1'] = 'Model Assumptions'
assumptions['A1'].font = Font(bold=True, size=14)

assumptions['A3'] = 'Revenue Growth'
assumptions['B3'] = 0.15
assumptions['B3'].font = Font(color='0000FF')
assumptions['B3'].fill = PatternFill(start_color='FFFF00', end_color='FFFF00', fill_type='solid')
assumptions['B3'].number_format = '0.0%'

assumptions['A4'] = 'Gross Margin'
assumptions['B4'] = 0.65
assumptions['B4'].font = Font(color='0000FF')
assumptions['B4'].fill = PatternFill(start_color='FFFF00', end_color='FFFF00', fill_type='solid')
assumptions['B4'].number_format = '0.0%'

assumptions['A5'] = 'Tax Rate'
assumptions['B5'] = 0.21
assumptions['B5'].font = Font(color='0000FF')
assumptions['B5'].fill = PatternFill(start_color='FFFF00', end_color='FFFF00', fill_type='solid')
assumptions['B5'].number_format = '0.0%'

# Sheet 2: Income Statement
income = wb.create_sheet("Income Statement")
income['A1'] = 'Income Statement'
income['A1'].font = Font(bold=True, size=14)

years = ['2024', '2025', '2026']
income['A3'] = 'Year'
for idx, year in enumerate(years, start=2):
    income.cell(3, idx, year)
    income.cell(3, idx).font = Font(bold=True)

# Revenue
income['A5'] = 'Revenue'
income['B5'] = 1000000
income['B5'].font = Font(color='0000FF')
income['B5'].number_format = '$#,##0'

# Years 2-3 with growth from assumptions sheet
income['C5'] = '=B5*(1+Assumptions!$B$3)'  # Links to assumptions (green)
income['C5'].font = Font(color='008000')
income['C5'].number_format = '$#,##0'

income['D5'] = '=C5*(1+Assumptions!$B$3)'
income['D5'].font = Font(color='008000')
income['D5'].number_format = '$#,##0'

# COGS
income['A6'] = 'COGS'
for col in range(2, 5):
    col_letter = chr(ord('A') + col - 1)
    income.cell(6, col, f'=-{col_letter}5*(1-Assumptions!$B$4)')
    income.cell(6, col).font = Font(color='008000')  # Green for cross-sheet
    income.cell(6, col).number_format = '$#,##0;($#,##0);-'

# Gross Profit
income['A7'] = 'Gross Profit'
for col in range(2, 5):
    col_letter = chr(ord('A') + col - 1)
    income.cell(7, col, f'={col_letter}5+{col_letter}6')
    income.cell(7, col).font = Font(color='000000')
    income.cell(7, col).number_format = '$#,##0'

# Sheet 3: Balance Sheet
balance = wb.create_sheet("Balance Sheet")
balance['A1'] = 'Balance Sheet'
balance['A1'].font = Font(bold=True, size=14)

balance['A3'] = 'Year'
for idx, year in enumerate(years, start=2):
    balance.cell(3, idx, year)
    balance.cell(3, idx).font = Font(bold=True)

# Assets
balance['A5'] = 'Assets'
balance['A5'].font = Font(bold=True)

balance['A6'] = 'Cash'
for col in range(2, 5):
    col_letter = chr(ord('A') + col - 1)
    # Link to income statement profit * 0.3 (simplified)
    balance.cell(6, col, f"='Income Statement'!{col_letter}7*0.3")
    balance.cell(6, col).font = Font(color='008000')  # Green for cross-sheet
    balance.cell(6, col).number_format = '$#,##0'

# Sheet 4: Cash Flow
cashflow = wb.create_sheet("Cash Flow")
cashflow['A1'] = 'Cash Flow Statement'
cashflow['A1'].font = Font(bold=True, size=14)

cashflow['A3'] = 'Year'
for idx, year in enumerate(years, start=2):
    cashflow.cell(3, idx, year)
    cashflow.cell(3, idx).font = Font(bold=True)

# Operating Cash Flow (links to Income Statement)
cashflow['A5'] = 'Operating Cash Flow'
for col in range(2, 5):
    col_letter = chr(ord('A') + col - 1)
    cashflow.cell(5, col, f"='Income Statement'!{col_letter}7")
    cashflow.cell(5, col).font = Font(color='008000')
    cashflow.cell(5, col).number_format = '$#,##0'

wb.save('integrated_model.xlsx')

Recalculate:

python .claude/skills/xlsx/scripts/recalc.py integrated_model.xlsx

Result: Comprehensive multi-sheet financial model with proper linking (green color for cross-sheet references) and integration between statements.

docs.title: Investigation Documentation Templates
docs.text: This directory contains standardized templates for capturing investigation findings in persistent documentation.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: After completing investigations (code analysis, architecture reviews, system explorations), the knowledge-archaeologist agent can generate documentation using these templates to preserve findings for future sessions.

docs.title: 1. investigation-doc-template.md
docs.text:
Use for:

  • General code investigations
  • Bug analysis and root cause investigations
  • Performance investigations
  • Feature explorations
  • System behavior analysis

Sections:

  • Findings Summary
  • Architecture Diagrams (optional)
  • Key Files
  • System Integration
  • Verification Steps
  • Examples
  • Knowledge Gaps
  • Related Documentation

docs.title: 2. architecture-doc-template.md
docs.text:
Use for:

  • System architecture analysis
  • Component relationship mapping
  • Integration flow investigations
  • Design pattern documentation
  • Architectural decision records

Sections:

  • Findings Summary
  • Architecture Diagrams (overview, relationships, data flow)
  • Key Files
  • System Integration (with dependencies and patterns)
  • Verification Steps
  • Examples
  • Design Decisions
  • Future Considerations
  • Related Documentation

docs.title: Automatic Generation (via knowledge-archaeologist agent)
docs.text:
When completing an investigation, the knowledge-archaeologist agent will:

  1. Prompt: "Shall I create a permanent record of this investigation in the ship's logs (documentation)?"
  2. If accepted, select appropriate template based on investigation type
  3. Populate template with investigation findings
  4. Save to ~/.amplihack/.claude/docs/[TYPE]_[TOPIC].md

docs.title: Manual Generation
docs.text:
You can manually create documentation using these templates:

  1. Copy the appropriate template
  2. Replace all [PLACEHOLDER] sections with actual content
  3. Save to ~/.amplihack/.claude/docs/ with naming convention:
  4. ARCHITECTURE_[TOPIC].md for architecture investigations
  5. INVESTIGATION_[TOPIC].md for general investigations
  6. Use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for TOPIC (e.g., USER_PREFERENCES_HOOKS)

docs.title: Template Variables
docs.text:
Common placeholders in templates:

  • [TOPIC]: Investigation focus (e.g., "USER_PREFERENCES_HOOKS", "MEMORY_SYSTEM")
  • [FINDINGS]: Executive summary of discoveries
  • [DIAGRAMS]: Mermaid diagrams (system structure, data flow, relationships)
  • [FILE_PATH]: Absolute path to key file
  • [DESCRIPTION]: Purpose or role explanation
  • [TIMESTAMP]: Generation date and time

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: See ~/.amplihack/.claude/docs/ directory for examples of generated documentation.

docs.title: File Naming Convention
docs.text:
Format: [TYPE]_[TOPIC].md

Examples:

  • ARCHITECTURE_NEO4J_MEMORY_SYSTEM.md
  • INVESTIGATION_HOOK_EXECUTION_ORDER.md
  • ARCHITECTURE_USER_PREFERENCES_INTEGRATION.md

Rules:

  • Use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for visibility and consistency
  • Be specific but concise in TOPIC naming
  • TYPE is either ARCHITECTURE or INVESTIGATION

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Knowledge Preservation: Investigations aren't lost in chat history
  • Faster Onboarding: New contributors can read past investigations
  • No Repeated Work: Don't re-investigate the same systems
  • Documentation Growth: System documentation grows organically from investigations
  • Searchability: Easy to find and reference past investigations

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
These templates integrate with:

  • INVESTIGATION_WORKFLOW.md: Investigation workflow includes documentation step
  • knowledge-archaeologist agent: Primary agent for doc generation
  • analyzer agent: Source of investigation findings

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
To customize templates:

  1. Edit the template file directly
  2. Add or remove sections as needed
  3. Modify placeholder text for clarity
  4. Keep the basic structure intact for consistency

Templates should remain simple markdown with clear section headers and minimal formatting complexity.

docs.title: PRESENTATION STRUCTURE
docs.text:
When presenting these findings to the user, organize as follows:

1. Executive Summary (2-3 sentences) [One sentence on what was accomplished, one on key insight]

2. Key Findings Breakdown

  • Lead with 2-3 most important findings (what worked well + top improvement area)
  • Use specific examples from the session
  • Be verbose - include context and reasoning

3. Recommendations Summary

  • Present top 3-5 recommendations in priority order
  • For each: Problem → Solution → Impact
  • Be verbose - explain WHY each recommendation matters

4. Action Options Present these specific options to the user:

a) Create GitHub Issues

  • For high-priority recommendations
  • Option to work on them NOW or LATER
  • List which recommendations warrant issues

b) Start Auto Mode

  • If there are concrete improvements that can be implemented immediately
  • Describe what would be automated

c) Discuss Specific Improvements

  • If user wants to explore certain recommendations in detail
  • List which ones are good candidates for discussion

d) Just Stop

  • If user is satisfied and wants to end session
  • Remind that next stop will succeed (semaphore prevents re-run)

Usage Instructions:

  1. When to Use: End of significant sessions (not trivial tasks)
  2. Who Fills It: Reflection system or manual session review

docs.title: Investigation Summary Template
docs.text: Use this template to document comprehensive investigation results that include both success paths AND failure scenarios.

docs.title: Why This Template Exists
docs.text:
Problem: Previous investigations focused on "how it works" without addressing "what could go wrong", edge cases, error handling, or limitations. This led to incomplete investigations requiring follow-up questions.

Solution: This template mandates comprehensive coverage of both architecture AND robustness, ensuring one-and-done investigations that users can rely on for production decisions.

docs.title: Quick Reference Template
docs.text:
Copy this structure and fill in each section:

# Investigation: [System/Feature Name]

## 1. Architecture Overview

[High-level system design, components, data flow]

## 2. Key Components Deep Dive

[Detailed analysis of each component]

## 3. Integration Points

[How system connects to other systems]

## 4. Edge Cases & Error Handling ⭐

[What happens when things go wrong]

## 5. Known Limitations

[What system doesn't do or constraints]
